      <title>Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/16/vw-ford-tesla-batteries-deforestation-indigenous-lands</link>
      <description><p>Mines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in Indonesia</p><p>Volkswagen, Ford and Tesla are among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction.</p><p>Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot in Indonesia that houses the world’s largest nickel deposits. The metal is widely used in cathodes in car batteries because it boosts energy density and increases range.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/16/vw-ford-tesla-batteries-deforestation-indigenous-lands">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>People in the US: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/what-is-your-personal-recession-indicator</link>
      <description><p>We’d like to hear about whether you feel like the US is in a recession and what you think signals such a downturn</p><p>Nearly two-thirds of Americans think the US is experiencing a recession, according to a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/voters-economy-cost-of-living-prices-poll">new Harris Poll</a> conducted for the Guardian. By the typical definition of a recession – when a country’s economic growth is in the negative for two consecutive quarters – the US is not experiencing one. Still, Americans are facing <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/14/inflation-numbers-september">higher prices</a> and a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/02/september-jobs-report">stagnant job market</a>, which for many feels like a downturn.</p><p>We want to hear from Americans: do you feel like the US is experiencing a recession? What is your so-called personal “recession indicator”, or a signal in your everyday life that points to an incoming economic slump? It could be seen in your job or at your local grocery store, something you notice at your children’s school or out in your community. Tell us about it below.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/what-is-your-personal-recession-indicator">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Voters’ opposition to the state of Trump’s economy is well established – despite his desperate attempts to deflect</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/what-is-your-personal-recession-indicator">Tell us: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?</a></p></li></ul><p>It’s indisputable that the political polarization of our time has reduced (and confused) the influence of economic conditions on US elections.</p><p>In September of 2024, in the waning weeks of the Joe Biden presidency, 65% of Republicans believed the US economy was getting worse.       <link>https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oct/15/food-delivery-apps-cost-economy</link>
      <description><p>As Americans use apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats more habitually, they confront the guilt of paying extra fees for convenience</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/what-is-your-personal-recession-indicator">Tell us: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?</a></p></li></ul><p>When it comes to food, Caroline Bauldree does not like to “deprive” herself of anything. She does not like to cook either, so that means a lot of food deliveries. “If I want sushi, I’m getting sushi,” said the 24-year-old nanny, who lives in Raleigh, North Carolina. “I’m definitely lazy in that regard.”</p><p>Bauldree got into the habit of near-daily DoorDashing back in college. “I could order whatever food from whatever restaurant and it showed up at my door – that’s the dream,” she said. “But then I just feel like crap about myself because I’m like, ‘wow, I’m a lazy piece of shit.’ Nine times out of 10, I feel bad about myself.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oct/15/food-delivery-apps-cost-economy">Continue reading...</a></description>

    <item>
      <title>Is punishing the poor Trump’s last hand to play?</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms</link>
      <description><p>The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees looks like political madness – but the president appears to believe hitting poor people might work for him</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/community/live/2026/oct/14/us-economy-affordability-midterm-elections-republicans-trump">Our reporters answer your questions on whether Trump’s economy will sink Republicans in the US midterms</a></p></li></ul><p>There is a manic quality to <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/us-midterm-elections-2026">midterm elections</a> to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away.</p><p>The US president <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/28/trump-cattle-ranchers-beef-imports-backlash">offered</a> to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/23/trump-beef-imports-midterms-gop-panic-01090261">backtracking</a> under <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/25/trump-republican-backlash-beef-tariff-import">pressure</a> from the cow lobby. He <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/22/trump-diesel-export-ban">offered</a> to stop diesel exports, only to find oil companies <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/market-chatter-us-oil-executives-112235250.html">were</a> <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/chevron-ceo-diesel-export-ban-trump-supply.html">not interested</a>. He weakened fuel efficiency standards, claiming this would trim the price of a new car (and forgetting to point out it will also raise spending on gas). In early October he started mailing <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/01/economy/trump-obamacare-500-check">$500 checks</a> to nearly a million people touting his healthcare “wins”. Oh, and he promised adult Americans a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-5000-midterm-cash-dividend-response">$5,000 check</a> if Republicans maintain control of Congress. That, too, will <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-dividend-republican-midterm-convention">go nowhere</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comSun, 18 Oct 2026 12:40:07 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Leaving shares to a spouse at death can make more sense than a lifetime transfer ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/18/leaving-shares-to-a-spouse-at-death-can-make-more-sense-than-a-lifetime-transfer/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/18/leaving-shares-to-a-spouse-at-death-can-make-more-sense-than-a-lifetime-transfer/Sun, 18 Oct 2026 09:00:00 +0000I own shares in a company which, if sold today, would attract a large tax liability. In one of your articles, you state that “section 1028 of the Taxes Consolidation Act provides that no capital gains arises on assets that are given by one spouse to another”.

So if I transfer my shareholding into my wife’s name, I am no longer liable for capital gains tax (CGT) in that shareholding and my wife’s tax liability commences from the time she receives the shares until the time she eventually sells them. Is that correct? Is the transfer to my wife by way of a gift? Does gift tax arise?

Does the share transfer require new share certificates to be issued in my wife’s name? If so, is this a simple matter? Are there any fees involved in such a transfer?

In the event of my wife’s death, these shares would become part of her estate and would not attract CGT. Is that right?

I understand from your article that if my wife died before me and she left the shares to me, I would again be liable to large capital gains liability. Should my wife indicate in her will that these shares should pass to my daughter, would this resolve the above issue?

DS

Investing in individual stocks is clearly a high-risk game as all your eggs are in one basket rather than being diversified across a number of shares or other assets in an exchange trade fund (ETF). However, stock markets have enjoyed a very strong run in recent years and, for those who chose wisely (or fortunately), their investments have secured strong gains.

And that raises the issue of tax planning.

None of us wants to pay any more tax than we are required to and, as that recent letter to which you refer highlighted, there are potentially valuable exemptions that can help couples do this.

When budget changes kick in and how to claim them

Irish law determines that gifts (and inheritances) between spouses do not attract any capital acquisitions tax (CAT) liability. So anything your wife gives you or you give your wife is exempt from this tax, which is more commonly known as inheritance tax or gift tax.

You ask whether the transfer you are considering would be seen as a gift? It will, yes, but not one that is liable for gift tax.

At a practical level, you sensibly raise the issue of share certificates or, in more recent times, an electronic record of share ownership.

Registrars are companies that manage the share registers of listed companies. Most particularly, they keep track of who owns how many shares and record changes of ownership when shares are sold or otherwise transferred.

They also keep shareholders notified of company events, such as annual meetings, share placings, rights issues, consolidation, or special meetings to approve things like takeovers, etc.

There are a number of companies that specialise in this work. You do not identify which company’s shares we are talking about here so I cannot tell you which one you need to approach, but the information will be readily available in the investor relations section of the website of the company you’ve invested in.

You can also get the details from any email or letter they may have sent you.

They will send you a share transfer form to formalise the transfer of ownership of these shares to your wife. There will be a charge to do this. I cannot say precisely how much this will be but it tends to be fairly nominal.

If you do not have your share certificate, things can get a bit more costly as you may need to sign (and pay for) an indemnity letter.

The whole thing is a fairly straightforward process though it can be slightly bureaucratic and stressful for people unused to dealing with share registrars, a group which, by the nature of their work, tends to communicate in fairly formal legal terms.

Capital gains tax

But what about CGT? By your own admission, you have built up quite a CGT liability on these shares over time.

This was the gist of the previous question and, as I said then, the transfer to your wife does not trigger any CGT bill. However, that does not mean that the capital gain you have made disappears; it just transfers to your wife.

While neither of you has any tax bill to pay right now, your wife is deemed to have acquired the shares not on the date you transfer them to her and at their price on that day, but on the date and at the price you originally acquired them for.

If she sells them down the line, all you have really done is transfer your large CGT bill to her.

But what about if she holds them until she dies? Well then, as I said in response to the previous query, the capital gain will die with her. Any capital gain dies with the owner of an asset.

Whoever succeeds her in owning these shares will not have to worry about the legacy capital gain dating back to the time you originally acquired the shares. The only capital gain that will apply for new owners will be the difference in the price when your wife dies and the price at which they eventually sell the shares.

This, as another reader found recently, can create unexpected tax liability as probate generally takes a year and, in strong equity markets, people can find themselves unwittingly with an outstanding capital gain the moment they actually get access to shares. For the new owner, capital gains does not start with when they get control of the shares but when the previous owner dies.

Inheritance tax reform could unlock €170bn sitting on deposit, expert says

There is one area where you appear to have confused something I have mentioned previously. You understand that if your wife were to leave the shares to you when she dies, the clock goes back to when you originally bought these shares. That is not so.

If your wife were to subsequently transfer the shares back to you while alive, yes, that is the case. But not if she leaves them to you in her will or even in the absence of a will.

Whether your wife leaves these shares to you, her daughter, or anyone else, no CGT issue arises. She can mention them specifically in her will, she can simply leave them to be dealt with under a residuary clause – a clause all wills should have dealing with assets not otherwise allocated to a specific beneficiary – or they can be dealt with under intestacy. In none of those cases will capital gains arise, even if she leaves them to you.

What may arise is our old friend CAT.

Anything your wife leaves you in her will or anything you otherwise inherit from her is free of inheritance tax but that is not the case for her daughter or any other beneficiary.

The budget raised the amounts anyone can receive in inheritance without paying tax. For a child inheriting from a parent, this threshold is now €420,000. That will cover anything your daughter inherits from either parent and also any gift they may have received from you in your lifetimes over the value of €3,000 in any one year.

But at the end of all this, I have one question for you?

If the intention is not to sell the shares, why bother with this lifetime transfer? If you sell the shares or you transfer them to your wife and she sells them, the same CGT bill arises – and in most families will be paid from the common family financial pool.

And if either of you dies owning the shares, no CGT applies.

Inheritance tax in Ireland: ‘The rules are absolutely skewed against the childless’

The only real financial benefit here is if your wife dies before you, having taken ownership of the shares, and then leaves them to you in her will. That would wipe out your CGT liability for sure.

But demographics suggest that a woman will live longer than a man in Ireland, even these days. And it would seem to benefit her more when considering tax exposure to receive these shares from you via your will when she does not have to worry about any tax bill – CGT or CAT.

]]><![CDATA[Human resources doesn’t need to be the CIA ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/18/human-resources-doesnt-need-to-be-the-cia/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/18/human-resources-doesnt-need-to-be-the-cia/Sun, 18 Oct 2026 09:00:00 +0000What would you think if you were asked in a job interview to hold up three fingers in front of your face? Perhaps you’re doing so badly that they’re checking you’re not concussed?

More likely the recruiter is trying to check that you’re not an artificial intelligence (AI) deepfake.

Employers are trying all sorts of things to combat fraudulent AI use in the recruitment process. There are jobseekers who use chatbots to bluff their way into jobs they’re not capable of, or pay “interview mules” to complete assessments for them.

More dangerously, there are hackers who try to get hired with false identities in order to access internal systems, and even remote information technology (IT) workers who turn out to be based in North Korea. The research company Gartner has predicted that one in four candidate profiles worldwide will be fake by 2028.

All this is leading to a culture clash inside companies. The warm and fuzzy realms of human resources (HR) and recruitment are having to learn to work with the suspicious minds of the cybersecurity world.

One example: the HR platform Deel acquired AI cybersecurity company Clarity in August in order to “embed continuous identity security across the entire hiring and workforce life cycle”.

Neev Wilf, who was at Clarity and is now head of product at Deel Security, tells me that “bringing HR and security to the same room is tough” because they “have different interests”. Security teams usually want “every protection, every feature, all the way” but “at the same time, you have [recruiters] who say ‘this enhances friction for the candidate’”.

What sort of security checks are we talking about here? Recruitment platform Greenhouse has introduced a system to allow employers to prompt job seekers for ID verification. “Some do it at the top of the funnel, in the beginning of the process, and some do it further down,” Daniel Chait, Greenhouse’s chief executive, tells me.

A recent study of executive pay finds that enormous share awards usually fail to deliver for shareholders and that “milestones are far less demanding than they appear”, with Musk’s 2025 Tesla package offering a striking illustration of the risks.

In Merging to the Moon: Astronomical Option Awards and Corporate Governance Failures, researchers examined 1.24 million insider stock awards between 1996 and 2022. They found that Tesla-style “mega-grants” subsequently underperformed comparable companies by 15 to 30 per cent over following years.

Tesla’s 2025 agreement offers Musk 424 million shares if the company reaches an $8.5 trillion market value and meets 12 demanding business milestones.

Considered in isolation, the package looks like a properly designed pay-for-performance deal. Under the researchers’ modelling, annual growth of 12 per cent in both Tesla’s share price and earnings would leave the company just short of its profits target after a decade.

If only one operational milestone was met (cumulative vehicle deliveries), Musk would get a payout of about $8 billion – a big sum, yes, but a fraction of the headline award.

However, if Tesla is acquired, the agreement completely waives the operational targets. If Tesla were taken over, the same share-price growth could deliver Musk $448 billion to $545 billion at a typical 20-30 per cent takeover premium, or up to about $707 billion at a 50 per cent takeover premium.

In other words, Musk could bag up to 88 times what he would earn on the operational track, without meeting a single operational goal.

As Tesla sales tank, Musk gains a trillion-dollar pay day

The pay deal “converts a performance award into a transaction bonus”, potentially allowing Musk to engineer a takeover through an affiliated company such as SpaceX, triggering a huge payout while bypassing the operational targets.

Perhaps Musk’s greatest feat of engineering is financial rather than technological: the salesman who persuaded more than 75 per cent of shareholders to back a pay deal that has “essentially no analogue in market practice”.

Insurer Outsurance this week estimated that many homeowners could be undervaluing the cost of rebuilding or replacing their homes by about €83,000

Underinsurance can very quickly turn a drama into a financial crisis. Bad enough to have your home hit by flood, fire or other catastrophe without discovering your insurer will not cover the cost of putting things right.

People assume that if they have, say, €400,000 of insurance cover, any claim up to that value will be met. But that’s not the way it works.

If the cost of rebuilding your home is €600,000 but you only have cover for two-thirds of that (€400,000), the insurer will only cover two-thirds of every claim – even one for say €20,000 to repair flood damage – leaving homeowners thousands of euro out of pocket.

No one actually knows how pervasive the problem is.

Back in 2021, the Central Bank of Ireland sent a shot across insurers’ bows after a study by its staff discovered the level of underinsurance had surged from 6.5 per cent in 2017 to 16.5 per cent – not far short of 400,000 homes.

That figure, like the Outsurance average, emerged only from an analysis of actual claims made. We have no way of knowing how many others are underinsured. That’s not helped by the insurers themselves, Outsurance included, being remarkably coy on the subject.

In answer to a parliamentary question late last year, then minister for finance Paschal Donohoe said the figure had fallen to 10.7 per cent in 2024. Even if that claim reflects the wider market, there are still more than 230,000 homeowners at risk.

As Bank of Ireland noted in 2026, the trend over recent years to invest in upgrading and extending properties, including retrofits, solar panels and the like, could be making things worse.

All increase the rebuilding cost in case of disaster, but the bank found that six in 10 homeowners never update their insurance details after investing to improve their homes.

With winter looming, now would be a good time to make sure you have the cover you think you have ... before anything goes wrong.

Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment, Peter Burke, increased the financial values at which mergers must be notified to the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) in July.

However, his department has confirmed that Burke’s order lapsed on September 30th, when it emerged that the Oireachtas had not approved it on time, exposing deals agreed or completed since that date to possible investigation by the commission.

The ministerial order increased the financial threshold at which mergers must be notified to the commission to a combined turnover of €100 million or more, from €60 million.

Competition law obliges the CCPC to investigate deals meeting the threshold to ensure they do not damage competition in their relevant markets, before approving them, often with conditions meant to protect competition.

As the order lapsed on September 30th, the old rules have applied since then.

So mergers or takeovers agreed or completed since then, where the parties’ combined turnover is €60 million or more, and two of those involved have sales of at least €10 million each, may face investigation by the commission.

The CCPC is advising businesses involved in transactions either agreed or completed since September 30th to consider if they meet the old threshold and whether they should notify it of the deal.

The commission pledged not to investigate any parties to deals done in those circumstances for “gun jumping”, that is completing the transactions before getting its approval.

Any mergers completed between July 1st and September 30th were subject to the increased threshold, that is a combined turnover of €100 million or more, and at least €15 million for two of the parties involved.

According to the department, Burke’s order increasing the threshold was laid before the Oireachtas, but did not get the approval of both the Dáil and Seanad within the time set out by the Competition Act, 2002.

“As a result, the order ceased to have effect,” said a spokeswoman, who confirmed that the error emerged following a department review.

The Act requires the CCPC to investigate mergers for their likely impact on competition, but gives the Minster the power to raise the thresholds for such inquiries to keep them in line with inflation and economic circumstances.

Ministerial orders, also dubbed statutory instruments, generally need Oireachtas approval before taking effect.

Burke signed the order on June 10th, branding the move part of his efforts to cut red tape for business.

The Minister said at the time that he increased the financial notification threshold in response to a public consultation that he held earlier this year.

The CCPC favoured an increase as it allowed the regulator to focus resources on deals more likely to have a meaningful impact on competition and consumers.

The last increase was in 2019, before the significant inflation that followed Covid and the war in Ukraine.

The commission has the power to “call in” transactions below the €100 million value where it believes they could affect competition.

]]>Jade W <![CDATA[How Ireland’s first national public sector strike in 17 years left unions strong and Jack Chambers ‘scrambling’]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/politics/2026/10/17/strike-success-leaves-unions-in-position-of-strength-and-jack-chambers-scrambling/https://www.irishtimes.com/politics/2026/10/17/strike-success-leaves-unions-in-position-of-strength-and-jack-chambers-scrambling/Sat, 17 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000Perhaps nobody in Government had heard the old sales business adage: the first one to name a price always loses.

A decade’s worth of talks and deals that followed, from 2010 to 2020, are characterised as “defensive” by one senior trade union leader.

This, they felt, was given based on arguments that would not stand up to the scrutiny their own spending proposals are subjected to. “What you had there,” says one observer on the union side, “was people who went, parked their tractors and trucks and said, ‘right, we have the country by the balls’.”

Another person with a vested interest points to “unelected people suddenly having access to the highest levels of Government and being able to force changes that in some cases had been agreed with elected representatives or people with a respect for democratic structures”.

“Say what you want,” says the first observer, “but unions are regulated, there are rules they have to observe and they do because of the potential consequences.”

Most workers – many in modestly paid jobs and feeling the pinch of rising grocery, fuel and accommodation costs – were more put out by the expiry of the last pay deal in June.

It came at a time when prices were on an upward trajectory but the Government had not indicated when they might get around to ensuring their wages were raised accordingly.

Predictably, there is now something of a blame game as to why talks on a new agreement were delayed beyond the expiry of the last deal in June. What is undisputed is that a couple of exploratory meetings in June went poorly.

By the time Chambers wrote an opinion article in The Irish Times on July 1st, he was suggesting “all issues of importance to both sides can and should be discussed as part of any engagement”. One of those familiar with the process on the Government side suggests the unions wanted a final outcome on the pay issue before anything else could be discussed.

This, they argue, would have left the negotiators on the employer side with no leverage at all as they sought improved productivity through changes to work practice around artificial intelligence (AI), hybrid working or anything else.

The unions express exasperation that Chambers did not intervene directly, pick up the phone or arrange to meet them.

Those with experience of previous pay-agreement negotiations suggest there would traditionally have been more going on by way of back channels.

Callinan’s repeated calls this week for Taoiseach Micheál Martin to get involved are likely rooted in this, it is suggested by veterans of the pre-crash system of engagement during the “social partnership” from 1987 to 2009. Martin, they observe, is the only survivor on the Government side of how that worked and they would like to see his department reassert the control it used to exert over the negotiations.

Martin taking over might not look good for Chambers. However, Callinan made it clear on Friday that the shape of the preliminary talks process was hammed over a call with the Taoiseach.

The unions believe they are in a good position as the process gets under way, given how well Wednesday’s strike went.

Having energised this young and important constituency, he says the unions need to ensure they do not leave disappointed and disillusioned.

At this juncture, the unions might have felt it was better to threaten a second strike date than carry through with another stoppage – especially on what is forecast to be a cold and rainy day next Wednesday.

To get this far, he has repeatedly said that pay can be talked about at the outset, while the unions have stuck to their position: “Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed.”

Negotiating a deal that is good for the Government will still be a challenge, though.

Both sides point to different time periods, framing the relationship between pay and inflation in recent deals in a way that suits their purposes.

The unions do not want the sacrifices forced upon them in the wake of that strike 17 years ago to be written out of the equation.

Union leaders now talk about insuring their members against future spikes in inflation such as those caused by the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

However, such a mechanism would severely undermine the big prize from the negotiations for the Government: budgetary certainty for the coming few years.

The answer, some observers suggest, could be a short-term deal to get over the current impasse and allow everyone to come back when the tensions have eased. An alternative would be an agreement with a robust review clause for pay.

Both sides will likely agree on one thing if there is to be a short-term agreement: they will want to avoid being back in this current stalemate any sooner than they have to be.

Other valuation metrics tell a similar story. Apple trades on 36 times estimated earnings, well above its five-year average of 27.

Apple is pricey not only relative to its own history but to all but one of its magnificent seven peers (Tesla, of course). It is a pronounced premium compared with Microsoft, which trades on 27 times estimated earnings, as well as to Amazon (24), Alphabet (22), Meta (22), and Nvidia (14). Sixty-eight members of the Eirebus workforce are foreign nationals and 43 of them benefit from the on-site accommodation.

The planning appeal said the foreign-national workers were recruited from India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nepal and “their accommodation needs have to be carefully managed to avoid ethnic tensions”.

Thomson said the three-year planning retention was required and would allow the applicant to look at alternative longer-term accommodation solutions.

For historical reasons, 65 ended up as the widely accepted retirement age, but for a large part of human history, there was no such thing as formal retirement. People simply worked until they became incapable of doing so.

We have Bismarck to thank for introducing the concept of a modern state pension in the 19th century, with the retirement age set at 70 – at a time when few enough people lived to see that age. It was also 70 when the Old Age Pensions Act came into force in Ireland in 1908.

The qualifying age was subsequently adjusted downwards to where we are today, although a report produced in May of this year for the Financial Planning Standards Board suggests that while it’s nominally 65, many Irish people now expect to work until the age of 70 to maintain their standard of living.

Almost 80 per cent of those surveyed also felt financially unprepared for retirement, with a critical knowledge gap between what they were putting into their pension fund and how much income they thought that fund would provide when the time came.

Money, or having enough of it, pretty much tops the lists of concerns voiced by those facing retirement. This is closely followed by anxiety about filling the time previously taken up by work.

“Money is terribly important and, in an ideal world, you would start thinking about it long before you retire, maybe seven to 10 years before the planned date, because the sanest and most tax-effective way to save for retirement is by contributing to a pension scheme,” says Paul Kenny, a veteran of the pensions industry and Ireland’s first pensions ombudsman, who now leads courses for the Retirement Planning Council designed to get people retirement fit.

“Things happen that can radically change when people retire, such as illness, redundancy or an accident,” Kenny says. “Then there are those who put things on the long finger and suddenly they’re facing retirement with no financial plan.

“But all is not lost. Last-minute additional voluntary contributions (AVCs) are an option. How much you can put in is limited by your income in the final year and how much you can claim against tax, but they’re worth considering,” Kenny says.

AVCs are supplementary payments into your pension fund. If you’re in your late fifties, you can get tax relief on as much as 35 per cent of your salary if you put it into your pension fund. Above 60, that percentage jumps to 40 per cent.

So if you have just turned 60 and are earning €90,000, with normal pension contributions of 6 per cent, or €5,400, you can put up to a further €30,600 into your pension, assuming you have it. For many, it is a way of beefing up retirement income in a tax-efficient manner if they come into a windfall, such as an inheritance.

“When you’re looking at your overall money picture, an awful lot also depends on what kind of pension scheme you’re in because, in some cases, if you’re already getting the maximum from a scheme, AVCs are not going to do you any good. So, you need to know what you’re in and the benefits,” Kenny says.

“Annuities and approved retirement funds (ARFs) may also come up when discussing retirement financial planning,” Kenny adds. Both are products related to after-retirement income, not saving for retirement.

“An annuity, which will guarantee a payment for your lifetime, will be bought from an insurance company with the money in your pension fund and will very much tie you to what are currently low interest rates. Annuities are based on life expectancy and bond yields, and if interest rates are low, bond yields are low, so you’re locking yourself into a low interest rate for life.

“With ARFs, rather than lock your money into an annuity at a point in time, it remains invested after your retirement, with the retiree drawing down a certain portion of the fund each year.

“It’s crucial how you invest the money because that’s what will determine the capacity to draw down over the rest of your life. So, it’s really important to get good advice.

“ARFs are generally run by insurance companies, and they’re investing in massive numbers of different assets all over the world, something you could never do on your own, and this spreads the risk. They pay you the monies you are drawing down and take care of things like PAYE. An ARF gives you flexibility; if you really need money, you can make a drawdown and pay the necessary tax.”

Kenny says that the one thing to watch with ARF investments is the charges.

“If you’re being offered ‘hello money’ in the form of a bonus allocation, be careful. There’s only one person paying for that. So, the message is to go for the lowest charges. Anything over 1 per cent should be viewed with suspicion.”

Assuming the money side of things is under control, the next burning question for many prospective retirees is what to do with their time.

The psychosocial infrastructure is the term used to describe what a community, such as a workplace, provides to the individual. For better or for worse, this means having colleagues, work to do, and company events to attend. Losing this infrastructure can be a difficult adjustment, especially for those who have been defined by their job (often those in senior positions and the professions) or in whose life work was the dominant feature.

Kenny suggests reframing “all the time I have on my hands” to see it as a bonus, not a negative. “You’re getting back 50+ hours a week and why would you sit there and twiddle your thumbs when there is so much you could do?” he says.

“First of all, some people still want to work, so explore the options. Can you continue to work with reduced hours or part-time at your existing company with less pressure?

“Often people don’t want to keep doing what they’ve done for years, but that shouldn’t be a deterrent to doing something else. It’s really a question of looking for what’s available. If someone is prepared to work voluntarily rather than needing paid employment, then that opens another avenue.

“Sharing your talents, life and work skills with others can be invaluable and it feels good to give back. There are many charitable organisations which would bite your hand off if you had the skills to revamp an outdated system or update a website, for example.”

Retirees often get asked to join a board and, for many, it’s a good way of staying in touch. However, Kenny raises a warning flag. “Check the number of subcommittees because what looks like a once-a-month commitment can suddenly become twice a week,” he says.

Kenny adds age-appropriate exercise into the retiree timetable and also something to keep the brain agile. Both learning a new language and taking up a musical instrument for the first time are seen as particularly good ways to challenge the grey matter.

“The education and training boards offer a huge variety of hobby and other courses, with many of them heavily subsidised and run during the day. Then there are the more formal courses at Third Level for those who want to go the academic route,” Kenny says.

“Then come the hobbies which split into things you do alone and things you do with other people. I know of a gentleman who retired at 76 having known nothing but farming all his life. His son convinced him to go on a retirement planning course, and since then he has taken up horticulture, baking bread, general cookery, hill walking, yoga and line dancing.

“The wonderful thing about any of these activities is that they bring you into contact with new people who have no idea about who you are based on what you used to do,” Kenny adds. “In a sense, you get your personal identity back, and maybe that’s still a 25-year-old trying to break loose.”

   <title>Huthis bauen Rakete unabhängig von Iran</title>
   <description>Im Zuge des Iran-Krieges, den die USA und Israel Ende Februar begonnen haben, ist auch der Konflikt im Jemen wieder eskaliert. Die von Saudi-Arabien angeführte Militärkoalition bekämpft die Huthis, die Miliz greift im Gegenzug täglich strategisch wichtige Ziele in Saudi-Arabien an, erst am Sonntag wieder.    <title>Protesttag mit 1.200 Festnahmen</title>
   <description>In Frankreich ist es am Samstag bei Protesten gegen die gestiegenen Lebenshaltungskosten zu einer der schwersten Unruhen seit Jahren gekommen. Die Regierung kam am Abend zu einer Krisensitzung zusammen und kündigte eine harte Vorgehensweise an. Many more municipalities in Poland will be allowed to charge a daily fee for tourists and other overnight visitors after a change to the law dropping environmental requirements for levying such charges.

Kraków, which received 8.7 million overnight tourists last year, had in particular been pushing for the change. However, Poland as a whole has seen a recent boom in visitor numbers, recording the EU’s second-fastest growth in the number of nights in tourist accommodation last year.

#Krakow #opłataturystyczna #ustawa 🚨🔥Z OSTATNIEJ CHWILI! 🔥🚨

📢 Prezydent RP podpisał nowelizację przepisów dotyczących podatków i opłat lokalnych, PIT oraz PCC.

🏨 Najważniejsze zmiany dla branży turystycznej dotyczą opłaty miejscowej i uzdrowiskowej.

🗓️ Od 2027 r. za jej… pic.twitter.com/9ATvENvNol

— Kraków (@krakow_pl) October 15, 2026

Until now, a “visitor’s fee” could be levied by municipalities with beneficial climatic features, “scenic qualities” and the capacity to accommodate people visiting to benefit from these attributes, as well as localities in areas with the status of a “spa protection area”. In practice, this largely applied to seaside and mountain resorts.

Kraków did charge a visitor’s fee between 2004 and 2015, but was subsequently unable to do so due to a toughening of environmental requirements. The city has long suffered from bad air pollution, though it has taken significant steps to tackle the issue.

Now, under new legislation proposed by the government earlier this year and signed into law by President Karol Nawrocki this week, the requirement for beneficial climatic features has been scrapped, meaning many more places will be able to charge the visitor’s fee.

 

From 1 January, municipalities with scenic qualities will be able to charge visitors up to 5 zloty (€1.14) for each night they stay in hotels, guesthouses and short-term rental accommodation for up to one month, a rise on the current maximum of 3.46 zloty.

Additionally, whereas previously only people visiting for the purposes of tourism had to pay, the fee now applies to all visits, including for work or health purposes, reports broadcaster TVN. People with significant disabilities, children with certified disabilities and their carers will be exempt from the fee.

In another change, fees will be collected directly by accommodation providers, who will be required to maintain detailed records, reports the Infor news service. Passing fees on in a timely manner will entitle providers to receive at least 10% of the money they collect.

Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026

In 2024, Kraków appealed to the government to be allowed to charge tourists a fee, noting that “overtourism leads to tensions and social discontent”, as the “local community suffers” and “residents increasingly feel like tourists in their own city”.

With its UNESCO-listed Old Town, Wawel royal castle, and former Jewish district of Kazimierz, Kraków is regularly named as one of Europe’s best tourist destinations. Last year, a record 16.25 million people visited the city, of whom 8.7 million stayed overnight.

While that is a boon to the local economy, it also often causes tensions with residents, who complain about noise and disruption. In 2024, the city created the new position of “night mayor”, whose role is to reconcile the needs of tourists, businesses and residents.

Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals of the type offered through services such as Airbnb.

Such accommodation has boomed in recent years, often prompting a backlash from local residents https://t.co/8MRfRWTDxd

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 3, 2026

Following this week’s change to the law, Kraków city hall confirmed that it would now again be able to collect a visitor’s fee “if the statutory conditions are satisfied and the municipal council adopts an appropriate resolution”.

The city’s recently elected new mayor, Łukasz Gibała, who will be sworn in next week, said before Sunday’s election that he was in favour of a tourist tax of at least 20 zloty per night, four times the new maximum.

“In western European cities there are rates of that size and higher,” Gibała said, quoted by financial news service Money.pl. “Maintaining the city in the face of the influx of tourists is costly. In Kraków, private business owners profit from tourism, whilst the city and its residents foot the bill.”

Poland as a whole has also experienced a boom in tourism. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-largest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation. Its increase of 7% was behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta (9.9%).

Poland’s interior ministry has withdrawn a proposal to make it a criminal offence, punishable by up to three years in prison, to provide support to migrants who are in the country illegally. The idea had prompted criticism from human rights groups and even opposition from within the government.

The interior ministry said the amendment had been intended to clamp down on migrant smuggling. But activists feared it would criminalise humanitarian aid, such as that provided to migrants who have irregularly crossed the border from Belarus.

Za udzielenie bezinteresownej pomocy migrantom nie będzie groziła kara do trzech lat więzienia. Po burzy, którą wywołała publikacja „Rzeczpospolitej” i po sprzeciwie resortu rodziny, MSWiA wycofuje się z pomysłu „karania za podanie posiłku”.https://t.co/Q0N52IMRVn

— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 15, 2026

Under current Polish law, anyone who facilitates the illegal stay of a person in Poland in exchange for financial or personal benefit can be jailed for up to five years.

However, this week, the interior ministry proposed an amendment that would also have penalised anyone who knowingly “enabled or facilitated” the illegal stay of someone in Poland, even if not for financial or personal benefit. The offence would have been punishable by up to three years in prison.

By Daniel Tilles

Poland will hold parliamentary elections a year from now. The outcome will decide who governs the country for the next four years – although, given how close the polls are, and with questions over coalition formation, it could also result in uncertainty, chaos, and even new elections being called.

Below, we explain how the elections work, which parties will be standing, what kind of outcomes are possible, and which issues may animate the campaign.

When will the election take place?

Assuming early elections are not called, the vote must take place on a non-working day in the last 30 days before the end of the current four-year parliamentary term, which began on 13 November 2023.

Because elections in Poland are held on Sundays, that gives four possible dates: 17, 24 or 31 October, or 7 November (though 1 November and 11 November, which are public holidays, are also theoretically possible).

It is the president, Karol Nawrocki, who will choose the date. He must do so no later than 90 days before the end of the current parliamentary term.

How does voting work?

The 460 members of the more powerful lower house, the Sejm, are elected through proportional representation, meaning that seats are distributed more or less on the basis of the share of the vote parties receive (using the so-called D’Hondt method for allocating seats from electoral lists put forward by each party). However, parties must receive at least 5% of the vote nationally to enter parliament (a figure that rises to 8% for coalitions of parties who stand on a single electoral list).

The 100 members of the upper-house Senate are chosen through a first-past-the-post system similar to how members of the US Congress or British House of Commons are elected, with the candidate in each district that receives the most votes winning the seat.

How is a government formed?

A government can only be formed if it can win a vote of confidence in the Sejm.

After the elections, the president designates a prime minister, who is tasked with forming a government – which would almost certainly be made up of a coalition of parties – that must then win a vote of confidence.

If they fail to do so (as happened in 2023), the Sejm votes to choose an alternative prime minister, who likewise must try to form a government that has the confidence of the Sejm.

Parliament has chosen @donaldtusk as Poland's new prime minister.

That paves the way for him to form a new government in the coming days, ending the eight-year rule of the national-conservative PiS party https://t.co/iZUKh2rxnP

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 11, 2023

If that fails, the president has a second chance to pick a prime minister, who must again win a confidence vote. However, whereas the previous two votes require an absolute majority (większość bezwzględna) to be carried, this time only a simple majority is needed, making it easier to form a minority government.

If this third and final attempt does not work, then parliament is dissolved and new elections are called.

Who is likely to form the next government?

At the moment, it is incredibly difficult to say. Polls suggest an even split in support between parties generally aligned with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition – which ranges from left to centre right – and the right-wing opposition. However, the 5% electoral threshold complicates the picture.

According to current polling averages compiled by Polish website eWybory and Politico Europe, Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) leads with 32%. One of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), is on 7%, while two others, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), are on around 3% and 1%, respectively. Another left-wing party, Together (Razem), which previously caucused with the ruling coalition but split in 2024, is on around 4%.

Meanwhile, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, is on 20%. Two far-right opposition groups, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have 14% and 9%, respectively. The right-wing Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which broke away from PiS this year, is at around 5%.

Rolling 30-day average support in polls for Poland’s main political parties (source: eWybory.eu)

If we treat those as two potential blocs, parties more or less aligned with the current government are on around 47% while the right-wing opposition is on 48%. However, PSL and Poland 2050 currently look likely to fall below the 5% threshold if they stand alone, meaning votes for them would not count. That would significantly harm Tusk’s chances of forming a new government. If Rozwój Plus stood alone and fell below the threshold, that would harm the opposition.

It is therefore likely that, as the elections draw nearer, parties that seem likely to fall below 5% will seek to join forces with other groups. In 2023, PSL and Poland 2050 stood together in the so-called Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance. But they have made clear they do not intend to do that again. That leaves them with limited options. They could join forces with KO on a single electoral list, but that does not guarantee that their voters will follow them. Indeed, some may baulk at voting for Tusk’s party.

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026

Meanwhile, there are some wildcards in the pack. KKP, led by radical-right extremist Grzegorz Braun, is shunned by the mainstream right for its antisemitism, anti-Americanism and sympathy towards Russia. PiS’s leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, has declared that he would not allow Braun to join government. Development Plus has taken a similar position. Both parties value relations with the US and the Trump administration, whose ambassador to Poland has reportedly pushed them to rule out working with Braun.

However, if KKP maintains its current level of support, it looks almost impossible for the opposition to form a parliamentary majority without it, meaning there would be a strong temptation to somehow work with Braun. Kaczyński’s determination to remove Tusk from power may outweigh his dislike of Braun and desire to keep the Americans onside.

The Together party – if it manages to pass the 5% threshold – could likewise represent a challenge for Tusk when forming a coalition, given that it has criticised the government for failing to keep promises on healthcare spending, public sector pay, and liberalising the abortion law.

 

There also remains the possibility of some elements from each camp joining the other side – either entire parties or individual MPs defecting – in order to help form a government.

PiS has long sought to tempt PSL to its side (and recent reports suggest that even President Donald Trump tried to persuade PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, to do so). It is conceivable that Rozwój Plus could work with parts of the current ruling camp, though its hatred of Tusk would make that very difficult.

All of the difficulties outlined above mean there is a significant chance that it will not be possible for anyone to form a government, necessitating fresh elections – something that has never happened before in Poland. If that happens, it would mean uncertainty and a lack of clear leadership at a time when Poland is facing major security challenges and a worsening fiscal situation.

What about the Senate?

The Senate, like the Sejm, is currently controlled by the ruling coalition. Indeed, Tusk has an even larger majority there than in the lower house, making it harder for the opposition to flip. Although the Senate is much weaker than the Sejm – and control of it does not determine who forms the government – it does have some powers that make it a useful asset.

It can slow down the passage of legislation, though not block it. The Senate also must approve the appointment of certain officials, such as the heads of the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) and the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), as well as the Commissioner for Human Rights (RPO).

In a rare clash between Poland’s two houses of parliament, in both of which the government has a majority, the Senate has rejected a candidate chosen by the Sejm to become the new head of the state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) https://t.co/QUsqfDNh4s

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026

The upper house is also required to approve proposals by the president to hold national referendums. This year, the Senate has twice blocked moves by Nawrocki to hold a referendum on EU climate policies.

In a situation where Tusk’s coalition controlled the Sejm, and was therefore still in government, but the right-wing opposition held the Senate, that would give the president a powerful tool to call referendums on policies important to him and the opposition.

To that end, there have been calls for the right-wing and far-right opposition to form a so-called Senate pact, of the type that Tusk and his allies used to win control of the upper house in 2019 and 2023.

What that means in practice is that the parties forming the pact agree to stand only one candidate between them in each of the 100 Senate districts, making it more likely that they will scoop up votes from supporters of all the parties in the pact and win the winner-takes-all contest.

What role will Nawrocki play in all of this?

Presidents are in theory expected to be non-partisan. In practice, however, they will seek to boost parties or coalitions aligned with them, and with whom it will be easier to work.

Since Nawrocki was elected last year, relations and cooperation between the president and government have reached unprecedently low levels. Within just 10 months, Nawrocki had vetoed more bills than any previous president in history over their entire terms. He has made it abundantly clear that he would prefer to work with a government formed from the right-wing opposition.

During his first year, President Nawrocki has transformed his office into a centre of resistance to the government and become a unifying figure for the fragmented right.

Nawrocki also continues to enjoy strong approval ratings among the conservative electorate, meaning that his presence during the election campaign could act as a boost for the opposition.

What issues are likely to feature in the campaign?

A major issue will be the question of sovereignty. The right-wing opposition accuses Tusk of being Brussels’ and Berlin’s lapdog, handing over ever more power to the EU and prioritising Germany’s interests over Poland’s.

The ruling coalition, meanwhile, argues that PiS is too beholden to the Trump administration and warns that the opposition is pushing Poland towards “Polexit” from the EU, which would leave the country isolated and vulnerable, as well as much poorer.

Those battle lines extend to security policy too, with the Tusk government shifting emphasis towards Europe as a defence partner but PiS insisting that only the US can truly guarantee Poland’s security. In one of his first policy announcements since being elected on Sunday, the new mayor of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has declared that he will withdraw official patronage of its annual LGBT+ equality march.

Łukasz Gibała, who has been supportive of LGBT+ rights in the past and has previously attended the march, argues that the event has become too “partisan”. He stood for election as an independent and has pledged to depoliticise city hall.

His decision does not prevent the march from taking place. But it means that it no longer has the official support of the city.

Kraków’s equality march, which was first held in 2004, draws thousands of participants when it takes place each year in May. The event is used to demand greater LGBT+ rights in Poland, which is ranked as one of the worst countries in Europe for LGBT+ people.

In 2021, the city’s former mayor, Jacek Majchrowski, became an honorary patron of the march. In 2024, his successor, Aleksander Miszalski, became the first mayor to attend the event, declaring that Kraków should be “a home for everyone”.

However, Miszalski was removed from office earlier this year in a recall referendum, necessitating a new election, which was won by Gibała. He beat Monika Piątkowska, who, like Miszaski, is a member of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

The day after his victory, Gibała was asked by local broadcaster Radio Kraków if he would continue city hall’s patronage of the equality march. The new mayor, who takes office next week, declared that he would not, saying he “will avoid sponsoring events that have a partisan character”.

“I have the impression that, over the past three years or so, the community that organises equality marches has simply become partisan,” said Gibała. “These are people who ran for parliament and local government on the lists of specific political parties.”

Gibała did not indicate who he was referring to. However, one of the organisers of the equality march in Kraków is Magdalena Dropek, who has three times stood as a candidate for The Left (Lewica), one of the groups in Tusk’s ruling coalition, in elections to the Polish and European parliaments.

 

Gibała emphasised that he has himself attended equality marches in the past “and does not regret it”. He was previously an MP for both KO (when it was known as Civic Platform, PO) as well as for the liberal Palikot’s Movement (Ruch Palikota), later known as Your Movement (Twój Ruch).

During the recent mayoral election campaign, Gibała told broadcaster TVN that, as an MP, he had supported the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships in Poland, and said that his views had not changed.

In fact, although the current government supports recognition of foreign-same sex marraiges, it has not changed the law in that regard. Polish law still does not recognise any form of same-sex union.

The government, aware that opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki would veto any change to the law, instead issued a regulation (which does not require presidential approval) empowering local authorities to transcribe foreign same-sex marriages into their registries.

Many municipalities, especially more liberal larger cities, have begun to do so (some even did before the regulation was issued). But others, especially in more conservative places, have refused to, often arguing that there are legal doubts around the issue.

Data provided to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) by the digital affairs ministry last week showed that 516 foreign same-sex marriages have so far been registered in Poland. The largest numbers were in Warsaw (209), Wrocław (73) and Kraków (46).

The standoff between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president.

Berek is now the fifth judge to take their oath without presidential approval. The previous four have been denied entry to the TK, and speculation is rife that the government may soon take action to ensure that the excluded judges are able to take up their positions.

PILNE 🚨 dr Maciej Berek złożył w Sejmie ślubowanie na sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego! pic.twitter.com/sZlzLnsL3M

Under Polish law, a new TK judge must swear an oath “before the president”. However, since Berek was elected to the TK by the government’s majority in parliament in early September, Nawrocki has refused to swear him in.

The president claims that Berek has not presented evidence that he meets the statutory requirement of having practiced as a legal counsel for at least 10 years. Berek says he has done so.

Nawrocki has also expressed his opposition to the fact that Berek has gone from serving in Tusk’s cabinet, where he was minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of policy, to becoming a TK judge.

Even some members of Tusk’s ruling coalition opposed Berek’s candidacy, saying that it contradicted the government’s earlier pledges to “depoliticise” the judicial system, including by banning anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge.

 

With no invitation from Nawrocki forthcoming, on Wednesday morning Berek instead swore his oath at a ceremony organised in parliament. He declared that he was directing the oath towards the president, despite Nawrocki not being present.

The development came a day after the Venice Commission, an advisory body to the Council of Europe on constitutional law, had issued an opinion effectively supporting the government’s position on the crisis around the TK.

The commission found that the Polish president should swear in TK judges chosen by parliament “without delay” and does not have the power to review their election. It added that, if the president refuses to receive a judge’s oath, they are justified in taking it without him being present.

The opinion was welcomed by Tusk and his government. However, Nawrocki’s spokesman, Rafał Leśkiewicz, pointed out that the Venice Commission’s opinions are advisory and not legally binding.

A government committee has urged the competition watchdog to launch a probe into the UK’s live music industry and the most “dominant firms”. The Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee said on 18 October it is “pressing” the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) to launch a full market investigation into the live music industry in [...]]]>

A government committee has urged the competition watchdog to launch a probe into the UK’s live music industry and the most “dominant firms”.

The Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee said on 18 October it is “pressing” the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) to launch a full market investigation into the live music industry in the country before the end of the year.

This follows the Committee setting out its concerns over dominant firms in a report in May when it initially asked CMA to investigate the live music industry before the end of 2026.

The Committee said it is particularly concerned about the market dominance of entertainment giant, Live Nation, the parent company of ticketing platform Ticketmaster.

According to the group of MPs, concerns were raised with the watchdog after ticket sales for Oasis’ reunion tour, where tickets were being sold for thousands of pounds.

“Despite the evidence presented by the Committee, the CMA has yet to announce a full market investigation,” the Committee said.

“The Committee is now repeating its call for urgent action to ensure fair competition and a live music industry that works for performers, grassroots venues and fans,” it added.

Watchdog pressed for ‘timeline of their next steps’

According to the report, Live Nation’s market position “raised red flags against all three of the CMA’s factors for assessing market dominance”, and the firm “directly controlled 58 per cent of the 23.1 million primary tickets on sale in 2025, rising to 66 per cent when sales controlled by affiliated companies were included.”

“Britain’s live music industry should reward talent, not simply market power. We found a climate of fear, barriers for artists and grassroots venues missing out,” Liam Byrne MP, chair of the Committee, said.

“It’s clear to us that the CMA must launch a full investigation for the simple reason that fans and performers deserve a fair deal – and they deserve it now,” Byrne said.

The committee said it is writing back to the CMA “asking for details and a timeline of their next steps”.

Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately has said the government needs to “take action in the Budget” to “back businesses to employ more young people”, referring the one million young people who are not in employment, education or training (Neets).

Talking to the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg on Sunday, Whately said the Labour party have “killed jobs” for the younger generation, with an increase of more than 174,000 young people unemployed.

Youth unemployment in the middle of this year hit an 11-year-high while the number of Neets crossed the 1m mark before dropping back. 

This follows an independent review into mental health conditions including ADHD and autism by the Department of Health & Social Care after a steep increase in diagnoses for mental health conditions linking to the rise in youth unemployment, particularly in children in young people, published 8 October.

When asked whether the Conservative parties “tough love message” is right, Whately said it is “incredibly distressing” for young people who are getting “rejected from jobs repeatedly “endless rejections” from job applications.

“On the one hand, we need more jobs,” Whately said. “But we are also saying we need to recognise the welfare system isn’t helping people who are struggling with their mental health and neurodiversity.”

Whately, referencing issues with the UK welfare system, said young people are getting “cash handouts” in Personal Independence Payments (PIP), a tax-free benefit people above 16 and up to State Pension age can claim for long-term physical or mental health conditions, which she said “in theory” people can work alongside claiming.

“In theory, many people really worry about taking up a job, or even taking up training, as they think they’re going to lose their benefits,” Whately said. “The reality is, the welfare system is deterring people from working who would be better off in every sense of the word to be working.”

When asked whether she thinks young people are “too soft”, the shadow work and pensions secretary said the jobs need to be there in the first place, but “we do need to send a strong message”.

Whately added young people need to be “speaking about what they can do, not what they can’t”.

The shadow Tory minister claimed many young people with conditions such as ADHD are being told “they should sign on as soon as they start school.”

“The welfare system is deterring people from working,” Whately said.

Healey looks to lower business costs of hiring young people

This follows City AM revealing on 14 October chancellor John Healey is drawing up measures to slash the cost of hiring under-25-year-olds at the Budget as the government looks to tackle the crisis of youth unemployment and ease pressures facing businesses

The move to tackle the number of young people not in employment, education or training (Neets) by reducing hiring costs is likely to feature in Healey’s statement on 28 October, sources told City AM.

Profits at the UK arm of publishing giant Condé Nast fell by more than a third last year, according to new figures published after the family that owns the Vogue publisher ruled out a sale. The publisher saw pre-tax profits excluding exceptional items plummet 36 per cent from £28m in 2024 to nearly £18m last [...]]]>

Profits at the UK arm of publishing giant Condé Nast fell by more than a third last year, according to new figures published after the family that owns the Vogue publisher ruled out a sale.

The publisher saw pre-tax profits excluding exceptional items plummet 36 per cent from £28m in 2024 to nearly £18m last year.

This follows the media group, which publishes glossy titles including GQ, Vanity Fair, and Tatler, booking £64m in proceeds following the sale of its UK headquarters, Vogue House, in Mayfair.

UK revenues fell 7 per cent from £75.9m to £70.6m, according to the publisher’s newly filed accounts, but an 18 per cent hike in international revenues, to £29.7m, kept total revenues nearly flat at £100m.

“Condé Nast remains profitable in the UK for another year,” a spokesperson for the publisher said.

“The change in the exact level of profit reflects a period of planned investment in customised client solutions,” they said.

Costs tied to restructuring at the company more than doubled year on year, from £1.9m to £4.3m.

The publisher said this hike was “primarily due to severance costs” and “reflects the outcome of an ongoing business restructuring plan by the Group to refocus editorial, commercial and business teams on the strategic goals.”

“There were no large restructures in the UK business in 2025. There were isolated instances of redundancy, but headcount remained flat as hiring continued across the business,” the spokesperson said.

“In addition, there have been changes to the pension scheme projections and wage inflation, which also impacted profit for this year,” they added.

Billionaire family rules out sale

This follows the chair of the Newhouse family holding company Advance that controls Condé Nast, Steven Newhouse, ruling out a sale of the publishing giant after long-running speculation over future ownership of the firm.

Newhouse told the Financial Times: “Maybe for a certain class of non-media owner, there’s a prestige to owning media properties.”

“But we’ve been a media owner for 100 years. So we’re not in it for the glamour.”

I am a Princess Fiona seeking her Shrek. My best chance of finding my lonely yet loveable ogre and getting our long-overdue Happily Ever After, as every DreamWorks fan knows, is in a swamp. Hackney Marshes and Walthamstow Wetlands have thus far failed to deliver the requisite calibre of hero, so this summer I headed further afield.

My swampy destination? Haraka Bog in Kõrvemaa, an appropriately wet landscape an hour outside Tallinn, a place where Estonia’s flag mirrors the white sky, blue water, and blackness of the soil.

Choose your bog

Estonia is famously flat. It is a country of coastal plains and open skies, which makes Kõrvemaa feel like a secret that the Earth has been keeping to itself. Protected forest, bogs and mires, eskers, valleys and still forest lakes – this is the landscape of fairytale where any kind of magic could happen. As we walked through the valleys and between the pine trees, my forest guide, Marilin Pehka, kept repeating: “Be silent. Nature is already telling you what you need to hear. You are already having a conversation with it.”

Bogs are ecosystems where organic plant matter does not fully decompose but is deposited as peat. They are climate change fighting miracles, trapping carbon for 10,000 years or more. And although bogs and swamps might have a bad reputation for being dirty or smelly, nothing could be further from the truth: they are complex, well-balanced habitats, rare and beautiful wetlands where specialised plants and ground birds thrive.

With an overcast sky, the water in Haraka Bog looked metallic and dark, with ripples circling out from the occasional plops or rain. I had clomped in blue plastic boots along the narrow boardwalk through the forest, listening to the wind shaking the trees and to the occasional twittering of the birds. And as I walked, I prepared mentally to strip everything off and surrender myself to nature. It wasn’t as if there were many spectators around.

It was bracingly cold, but my heart rate quickened and my mind became enlivened, too. It felt as if it were not just clothes that I had shed. With all my layers off, I could completely let go, swimming in the middle of the bog, in light rain, completely naked. With bog swimming, it seems that Estonians understand how to fully experience nature, that if you approach the water, or the forest, naked, vulnerable, and in your most natural state, you can be reborn time and again and face the world anew.

How to sauna in Estonia

Uuejärv Nature Retreat is on a nature reserve which was previously a Soviet-era military training base. Its rustic sauna is heated by a wood-burning stove. During a guided sauna session you experience vihtlemine, the practice of beating one’s own body with bundled birch or oak leaves, which boosts circulation and is certainly invigorating.

Where to stay

Accommodation inside Kõrvemaa is sparse. I stayed in one of the Kuuse Concept Houses (kuusemajad.ee), set within dense spruce and pine forest near the Sportland Kõrvemaa Hiking and Ski Resort. The cabins are built in a Scandinavian style that does not so much sit in the forest as belong to it, with floor-to-ceiling glass walls that dissolve the boundary between inside and out. You wake up to trees. You fall asleep to trees. The only sounds are the ones the forest makes, the creak of branches and whatever is moving through the undergrowth outside.

What to eat

Chef Ellery Powell might be Norfolk-born and -bred, but he moved to Estonia more than a decade ago, and he pays tribute to his adopted homeland in each meal he cooks for guests staying at the Concept Houses. He sources every ingredient within a 50 km radius in Körvermaa, and, often, from much closer: I picked golden chanterelles (kukeseen) on my walk in the forest, and Ellery sauteed them in butter before me. He also treated me to salmon tartare, carefully wrapped under an umbrella of Estonian clover; and seabass with a white wine sauce, sprinkled in dill. 

To understand a culture, you have to indulge in its cuisine. Food will mend the cracks whenever language is a barrier. And Ellery speaks ‘Estonian cuisine’ very well.

The Prime Minister has flirted with the idea of letting football fans drink alcohol on terraces again and it could have an impact on how we measure fandom, writes Ben McMahon. The Prime Minister has flirted with the idea of letting football fans drink alcohol on terraces again and it could have an impact on how we measure fandom, writes Ben McMahon.

Settle into your Wembley Stadium seat for today’s NFL game and you can roar on the Jaguars with a cool Coors in hand. Visit the Hill Dickinson Stadium in May for rugby league’s Magic Weekend and you can drink Guinness from a two-pint cup. Planning to visit those same stadiums on a England or Everton matchday, however? 

You’ll do well to slip a Shloer into the stands. 

As PM Andy Burnham flirts with lifting the ban on football fans drinking in view of the pitch, the contrast of alcohol’s position among sports offers a unique insight into fandom. Just as F1 drivers spray champagne, Wimbledon-goers sip Pimm’s and darts fans fling lager, every sport has its own rituals and unwritten rules. But what adds fizz to one fan experience can burst the bubble of another.

Businesses operating around sport must drill down into the distinctions. Even if Burnham relaxes the ban, brands can’t just think, “Great, now what can we sell to football fans?”. The most important question, as always, remains: “What actually adds value to the experience people have come for?”

Alcohol a fuel to the fire?

Football clubs enjoy a level of fandom that other sports would give their right leg for. A deep-rooted sense of community, belonging and, in some cases, tattoos, guarantees fan loyalty even through the biggest defeats. The Premier League in particular is one of modern Britain’s greatest exports.

But that tribalism has a darker side. In the 1970s and 80s, British football spilled into hooliganism and violence, with alcohol often adding fuel to the fire. 

Since the ban was introduced in 1985, the sport’s culture has changed. More than 5,500 arrests were recorded at league matches in the 1984-85 season; today, football-related police action equates to just four incidents per 100,000 attendees, and even the recent highly charged “Dockers Derby” between Millwall and West Ham recorded just six arrests. 

But has football moved far enough from its past behaviours to justify reintroducing the fuel that fed them? 

Raising a glass to innovation

Football’s tribalism hasn’t disappeared. It’s still what makes the sport so powerful. The Premier League hardly has a problem persuading people to turn up – but nor is its next generation of fans crying out for another place to buy a lager.

Younger audiences are drinking differently, if at all. They’re also expecting more from live entertainment, like stronger fan interactivity and digital integration. Putting alcohol back into the stands sounds great for drinks companies, but is it a good argument for the modern football experience? 

The 2022 World Cup in Qatar offered an interesting live experiment. The late decision to ban alcoholic beer sales from stadiums entirely made huge headlines at the time. However, on-site innovations, from fast-track entry gates to entertainment zones, still showed that a global football experience could appeal to fans across cultures without alcohol sitting at its centre.

Think outside the box

The debate offers a bigger opportunity to follow Fifa’s lead, look beyond the pint and ask what else could make the experience better.

Other sports are already making huge strides here. Cricket has introduced entirely new short formats in T20 and The Hundred, while NBA jumbotrons run live fan-focused segments like kiss cams and dance-offs during in-game lulls. Football itself tested a new Super Bowl-style halftime show at the recent World Cup final, plus activations and in-stadium augmented reality tools. 

The prime opportunity for businesses sits in that space around the sport. NFL-style tailgate parties, for example, could turn the hours before kick-off into somewhere fans meet, eat and spend time together – rather than a march from the pub to the stadium bar. It builds commercial value because it first creates something worthwhile for the audience.

The same principle applies to every type of sport. At Goodwood’s motoring festival, eBay Garage tapped into the knowledge of the crowd. It worked because it added to what people had come to enjoy, rather than competing with it.

Play the fandom occasion, not just the audience

Sponsorship can buy access to an audience but the key is understanding what makes that audience tick.The real test is asking what fans are turning up for. 

As this country’s national sport, top-flight football doesn’t have any issues attracting audiences. So any legislative decision that changes the fabric of the matchday experience must show a clear net benefit for the people watching it, rather than simply a commercial upside for the businesses selling into it. Brands need to hold themselves to the same standard.

Ben McMahon is the Global CEO of Collaborate
