]]>

Nicolas Sauvage, founder and president of TDK Ventures, with ANYbotics’ quadruped robot. | Source: TDK Ventures

A robot picks up an object, moves it, and puts it down successfully. Is it dexterous? Perhaps. But now ask it to do that successfully hundreds of times, while objects move slightly, its grip changes, components wear, and unexpected failures occur. That is a much harder test of dexterity, and a much better measure of whether a robot is dexterous enough for the real world.

We are making rapid progress in what robots can manipulate. However, useful dexterity isn’t simply the ability to complete an individual action once. It is the ability to sense, grasp, move, adjust and recover reliably enough to complete an entire workflow without constant human assistance.

A robot that succeeds 99% of the time sounds ready for work, but a job rarely consists of a single action. Consider a workflow that requires 100 physical actions in a sequence. At a 99% success rate for each action, the probability that all 100 succeed on the first attempt is just 36.6%. Increase the success rate to 99.9%, and the probability of completing the workflow rises to 90.5%. At 99.99%, it reaches 99.0%.

This is, of course, a simplified example that assumes equal and independent success rates, but it illustrates an important point. A robot with a 99% success rate is not necessarily 99% automated.

Small reliability gaps become much bigger when repeated across an entire workflow. This means that a robot that looks almost flawless in a demonstration can still be far from ready for autonomous deployment. The difference between two nines and four nines may ultimately decide whether a robot is ready to work alone.

The next major challenge in robotic dexterity is not simply teaching robots to do more, but making the entire system reliable enough to turn those capabilities into useful work.

Dexterity is a system, not a hand

Robotic dexterity is often discussed as a hardware race: more fingers, more joints and more freedom of movement. While those capabilities obviously matter, the customer does not buy degrees of freedom. The customer buys useful work.

Completing that work requires a closed loop across vision, position, contact, force, pressure, grasp, movement, and adjustment. Power, safety, flexibility, and recovery also matter.

Not every workflow needs touch, as in some cases, vision and movement data may provide enough information. But touch can also be useful in telling a robot that an object is slipping, the contact is unstable, too much pressure is being applied, or a component is properly in place.

The objective therefore isn’t to pile every sense onto every robot, but to give the system enough of the right information to act, and recover, reliably.

TDK Ventures helps early-stage materials, energy, cleantech, industry 5.0, mobility, and health tech startups scale. | Source: TDK Ventures

More nines come from learning

Recovery is a huge part of dexterity. If a robot begins to lose its grip on an object, the useful measure isn’t if the original grasp was perfect; it’s whether the system can detect the slip early enough to correct it before a small error causes the entire task to fail.

A failure discovered during deployment might expose a problem in software, sensing, or control, or it might reveal that the hardware itself needs redesigning. Changing the hand changes movement, sensing and calibration, so data collected with one physical design may not transfer directly to another. Real-world deployment is therefore a critical part of the development process.

Deployment reveals slips, poor grasps, wear, and failed recoveries. Those experiences become data that can improve software, simulation, sensing, control, and hardware. Each cycle can make the next deployment more reliable and less expensive.

A technological breakthrough may begin the journey, but it is the learning system around it that multiplies its impact. Robotic dexterity should be viewed in much the same way. Additional nines emerge from repeatedly deploying, learning and improving.

Editor’s note: Physical AI, enabling technologies, and humanoids are among the session track topics at RoboBusiness 2026, which will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif. Register now to attend.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

The right body depends on the work

Reliability also requires us to resist the temptation to equate more human-like robots with better robots. The starting point should be the job. From there, work backwards to determine the environment, physical form, and system required to perform it.

Dexterity should follow the same logic. The most human-like hand may not be the best hand for a particular workflow. The goal is not maximum dexterity. It is the minimum sufficient dexterity needed to complete valuable work reliably, and we are already starting to see this principle being successfully deployed.

Agility‘s Digit is a bipedal robot designed for logistics and industrial work. Digit can connect directly to specialized tools suited to the job, rather than requiring a five-fingered hand or being made to look as human-like as possible. It has the form and dexterity the work actually requires.

ANYbotics applies the same principle to a different environment. Its four-legged robots can navigate stairs and uneven surfaces at industrial sites, while inspecting hazardous areas reduces the need for human exposure. In one deployment, its technology has reportedly carried out more than 33,000 inspections across 450 inspection points.

Starship Technologies takes a different approach. Its delivery robots need to travel along pavements, so a small, wheeled form is better suited to the job than legs. That purpose-built approach has helped Starship to report more than 10 million autonomous deliveries.

These robots look and operate very differently because they perform very different jobs. Yet they demonstrate the same principle: The right physical form is the one that fits the work and can perform it repeatedly in the real environment.

Our investments in Agility, ANYbotics, and Starship have changed the questions I ask as an investor, particularly during our ongoing deep exploration into dexterity. I am less interested in which robot looks most human than in which complete system can reach the reliability its customer actually requires.

Sauvage with Agility Robotics’ Digit humanoid robot. | Source: TDK Ventures

Measure the job, not the demonstration

This changes how we should measure progress in physical AI. The success rate of an individual action shown in a demonstration tells us very little about whether a robot is actually ready to work autonomously in the real world.

I want to know what percentage of complete workflows finish without human assistance. When something goes wrong, how often can the robot recover without help? How does performance change when the object, lighting, position, wear or surrounding environment changes?

Then there are the less glamorous questions that become extremely important at scale. What breaks first under repeated use? How quickly can it be diagnosed, repaired and returned to work? What are the speed, uptime, and cost of each successfully completed job?

These are ultimately better measures of dexterity than what a robot can demonstrate once. A robot does not need the most human-like hand, the greatest number of joints or the widest possible range of skills to create value. It needs the right combination of physical form, sensing, control, and recovery to complete a valuable job reliably in the environment where it will actually work.

That is where I believe the next phase of progress in robotic dexterity will be won. The industry has made extraordinary advances in what robots are capable of doing. Now the challenge is turning those capabilities into systems that customers can trust to perform useful work repeatedly, recover when something goes wrong, and improve through deployment.

About the author

Nicolas Sauvage is the founder and president of TDK Ventures, the global corporate venture capital arm of TDK Corp. He launched the firm in 2019 around a simple principle: entrepreneurs come first.

Today, TDK Ventures manages $500 million across four funds and backs early-stage startups globally, across AI and compute, energy, industrial and robotics, mobility, and advanced materials.

]]> OMass Therapeutics, a UK BioTech company developing small molecule therapeutics against highly validated target ecosystems, announced an oversubscribed €275 million (£230 million) Series C round.

The round was co-led by new investors Bain Capital Life Sciences, Forbion and Novo Holdings, with additional participation from Janus Henderson Investors, SV Health Investors and Jefferson Life Sciences. Each of the Company’s existing investors also participated in the round, including Syncona, Oxford Science Enterprises, GV, Northpond Ventures, Sanofi Ventures, British Business Bank and University of Oxford.

“This financing comes at an exciting point in OMass’ evolution as we advance OMS1620 into the clinic, with our SLC15A4 inhibitor poised to follow,” says Ros Deegan, Chief Executive Officer of OMass Therapeutics. “We have demonstrated the ability of our team and approach to discover and deliver a pipeline of first- and best-in-class programmes in endocrinology and immunology into the clinic.

“With the backing of an outstanding group of new and existing investors, we are entering our next phase of growth with the resources to translate that progress into a portfolio of clinically differentiated medicines for patients.”

OMass’ Series C comes amid several significant European therapeutics funding rounds in 2026.

In France, Bionyra Pharma secured €143 million to advance treatments for inflammatory diseases, while Denmark’s Breye Therapeutics raised €67.5 million for its oral small-molecule pipeline, in a round also co-led by Novo Holdings.

In the UK, Cambridge-based STORM Therapeutics secured €47.5 million, Microbiotica raised €42 million, Glasgow-based Mironid received €39.9 million, and London-based Alchemab Therapeutics secured €29.3 million.

]]> Any founder who has raised money knows what investor due diligence feels like from the receiving end. The questions about the model, the customer contracts, the gap in your CV, the calls to people you worked with years ago. Investors do that work because they are making a long-term bet on your abilities.

However, the same isn’t true in reverse. In two decades supporting founders as they raise, I have found the majority could tell me everything about their own metrics, ambition for the business or ideal team hires, but very little about the people they approached for funding.

So, why is this? DocSend’s research on pre-seed rounds found founders contacted an average of 71 investors to close a round. Our own founder survey revealed a quarter of founders spend more than half their working week on fundraising. With so much time taken up, only about one in three do any serious research on investors. 

That can cost founders dearly. Months pitching investors who were never a fit for their stage or sector, time that should have gone into building, and potentially years unravelling a misaligned relationship. 

The market has made founders less likely to check

Today it is an investor’s market, and that is where the challenge starts. According to research, European startups did raise €21.41 billion ($24 billion) in the second quarter of 2026, two thirds more than a year earlier, but 65% of it went to just 42 companies raising €89 million ($100 million) or more, while early-stage deal numbers fell. When capital concentrates in fewer, larger deals, angels hold the leverage, and that is precisely when founders ask the fewest questions and most need the answers. 

Founders often tell me they cannot afford to be picky. They don’t have time for due diligence and asking too many questions or conducting background checks might put an investor off. I understand the pressure. Fundraising is fiercely competitive, and when capital is hard to secure, it can be tempting to pursue every opportunity that comes along. 

But this is precisely why a little research upfront matters. Knowing an investor’s criteria and track record tells you whether the approach is worth a week of your time at all. The ones you do pitch arrive at diligence already warm, and the process moves faster because of it.

What you are actually checking for

Start by deciding what you want from each investor. If you’re raising from 10 angels, for example, you might want two or three to take an active role, with the rest remaining silent backers. 

Then check the basics. Is this person who they say they are, and do they invest at the level and stage they claim? A depressing number of the conversations founders agonise over turn out to be dead ends.

Next, look at their track record. Which companies have they backed, which have they run, and where have they sat on the board? Sector experience matters more than general enthusiasm.

Then comes the step founders often skip because it feels too subjective: do you actually get on? We talk constantly about product-market fit, but much less about investor-founder fit.

Last comes alignment. Do you both want the same thing from this company, on a similar timeframe, with a realistic view of how it grows and how it might exit? Agreeing that at the start is what stops the relationship souring later. 

How to do it without interrogating anyone

Most of this work happens quietly, before the first meeting. LinkedIn, company websites and the public registers will tell you a great deal. In the UK, Companies House shows directorships and filings, and the European e-Justice Portal searches company registers across the EU. None of it takes any of the investor’s time, and none of it feels intrusive, because they never see it.

The most useful step is finding the companies an investor has already backed and speaking to those founders, through an introduction or by asking the investor for a reference. A founder who has worked with them will tell you more in 10 minutes than any amount of desk research.

Then stage it. Investors start broad and get more specific as they get closer to wiring the money, and founders can work the same way in reverse. References, personal checks and detailed KYC belong at the end, not on day one.

Use AI for the first pass, but human judgement for the verdict

Research that used to take days now takes minutes. Investors are increasingly using AI to manage and assess their dealflow, and entrepreneurs should be doing the same. 

I tested this for the first time recently on someone who I’ve known for years and was surprised by the level of detail that was produced, including certain information that I was previously unaware of and would have been unlikely to uncover with traditional online searches.

There are limitations, of course. Common names can return vague or misleading results, and everything needs to be fact-checked before you draw conclusions, positive or negative. Treat the output as a guide, not gospel. 

Trust your instincts as well as the record

If you have a feeling that something doesn’t seem right, trust your gut and do not ignore it. If an investor is moving unusually fast, pressing for information you are uncomfortable sharing, slow things down and dig further. It’s often a good idea to share your concerns with a colleague or friend to get a second opinion from an impartial outsider.

None of this should be seen as an extra stage bolted onto an already long process. It is what stops you wasting weeks on an investor who was never going to back you, and years with one you wish you had never taken. Investors will research you either way. The founders who do the same end up with backers worth having.

]]> Amazon Web Services (AWS) is preparing to test whether its European Sovereign Cloud can operate independently of foreign infrastructure – challenging if Europe can maintain greater control over its digital infrastructure.

This also marks a clear effort on AWS’ behalf to protect the brand against the rising demand in Europe to move past foreign-based tech and promote home-grown alternatives.

The exercise, scheduled for 24 October 2026, comes as Europe continue to attract investment to develop alternative cloud platforms, computing infrastructure and AI technologies aimed at reducing dependence on non-European providers.

The demonstration will take place at the AWS European Sovereign Cloud in Brandenburg, Germany, where the company plans to disconnect its infrastructure from the AWS Global Network backbone for several hours.

The operation will be carried out entirely by EU-based personnel using hardware and software resources located within the European Sovereign Cloud.

This test represents an attempt to provide technical evidence of operational autonomy at a time when European cloud sovereignty is receiving increasing attention from regulators, public institutions and investors.

Cutting the cord

The AWS European Sovereign Cloud operates from data centres physically and logically separated from the company’s other cloud regions. According to AWS, customer content and customer-created metadata remain within the EU, while a local copy of its source code allows the European operation to function with reduced reliance on external systems.

Under normal circumstances, the infrastructure uses two global systems: the AWS Global Network backbone, which transfers operational data between AWS locations, and a dedicated mechanism for managing limited transfers of operational information and software updates.

During the exercise, AWS will disconnect from the global backbone and disable the operational data transfer mechanism. Connectivity will instead be maintained through European internet service providers, enabling the cloud to remain connected to the worldwide internet without relying on AWS’s private global network.

The company intends to generate evidence aligned with the European Commission’s EU Cloud Sovereignty Framework and Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security’s C3A criteria. These frameworks address requirements for assessing the independence and autonomy of cloud services.

However, the demonstration will test a specific dimension of sovereignty: whether a major cloud provider can maintain operations within Europe without depending on infrastructure elsewhere. It will not, on its own, settle wider questions concerning corporate ownership, legal jurisdiction or customers’ dependence on individual technology providers.

Those are precisely some of the questions European startups are approaching from different parts of the cloud infrastructure ecosystem.

Europe’s home-grown stack

Across Europe, new companies are developing technologies that give businesses greater control over the infrastructure supporting their applications, data and AI workloads.

In September 2026, EU-Startups reported that Naples-based Clastix raised €2.9 million in Seed funding, for its Kubernetes infrastructure software that enables organisations to manage applications across their own computing environments. Its technology aims to reduce the operational complexity of cloud infrastructure while allowing customers to retain control over hardware and data.

Rather than operating its own sovereign cloud region, Clastix addresses the management layer, providing tools that can help organisations operate infrastructure without becoming dependent on a single hyperscaler.

A different approach comes from Cannes-based PoliCloud, who secured €7.5 million in 2025 to develop decentralised computing and storage infrastructure for cities, public institutions and enterprises. Its modular infrastructure can be deployed locally, offering an alternative to relying exclusively on large, centralised data centres operated by global cloud providers.

At the computing capacity level, Helsinki-based Verda, raised €100 million in April 2026 for its high-performance AI cloud infrastructure that gives developers and businesses access to computing resources at scale.

Its expansion reflects a broader European effort to develop computing capacity for increasingly demanding AI applications, although its international ambitions extend beyond Europe.

Meanwhile, Denmark’s Velatir, secured €5 million in August 2026 to develop an AI infrastructure and governance platform that helps businesses control how AI tools and agents interact with their systems.

The company says it has deliberately built its platform using European-owned and hosted infrastructure rather than relying on American hyperscalers.

Other startups are tackling adjacent challenges.

  • Prague-based Zerops raised €1.7 million in May 2026 for a cloud platform that brings development and production environments together, giving developers greater visibility and control over application deployment.
  • In Germany, Berlin-based Cognee secured €7.5 million in February 2026 for its structured memory infrastructure for AI systems, representing another layer of the wider European AI technology ecosystem rather than a direct sovereign-cloud alternative.

Together, the five 2026 financings give us a snapshot of €117.1 million in financing for companies looking to operate at different layers of the European cloud infrastructure ecosystem.

Sovereignty meets procurement

Beyond venture capital, European institutions are beginning to translate cloud sovereignty objectives into procurement decisions.

In September 2026, EU-Startups reported that Paris-based Cycloid would provide the developer-facing portal for the European Commission’s six-year, €180 million sovereign-cloud procurement framework.

Founded in 2015 by Benjamin Brial, a former Red Hat cloud executive, Cycloid develops an internal developer platform that enables organisations to access and manage cloud infrastructure, automation and development tools through a unified interface.

The European Commission’s framework, announced on 17 April 2026, provides access to cloud services through four European provider groups, including Post Telecom and its partners, STACKIT, Scaleway, and Proximus and its partners.

Cycloid’s technology is intended to give up to 5,000 European Commission developers a common interface for accessing these different providers, enabling institutions to manage workloads across multiple environments without depending on a single cloud platform.

Benjamin Brial, founder and CEO of Cycloid, said: “A sovereign cloud framework is only as sovereign as the choices it leaves open,”

Independence has layers

The sector context helps highlight that European cloud sovereignty is not a single technical challenge. It involves several interconnected questions about where computing infrastructure is located, who operates it, how data is managed, and whether customers can move applications between providers.

For European businesses and public institutions, the challenge is therefore not simply whether their data remains within EU borders. It is also whether they can maintain control over the systems that store, process and manage that data, and how easily they can change providers when requirements evolve.

AWS’s upcoming test may be enough to prove that its European Sovereign Cloud can operate without relying on non-EU infrastructure. However, it can also be read as an attempt soothe a growing distaste for reliance on foreign tech and protect the AWS brand.

“People said nobody could climb Everest without oxygen, until someone did. Reading hormones in saliva outside a lab has been our Everest. Women’s health rarely comes down to one hormone, so the Micro Lab is being built to read oestradiol, the main form of oestrogen, alongside three other key hormones simultaneously. 

The company says hormones shift throughout the month, but a blood test captures a single day. Wearables track every day but can only estimate hormone levels. It notes that the Micro Lab is designed to sit between the two, giving real hormone readings at home, day after day, at every stage of life from puberty to perimenopause,” the company mentioned in the press release.

Eva-Maria Dimitriadis, Managing Partner at Conduit EIS Impact Fund, said, “Women’s hormonal health is one of the largest under-served markets in healthcare, and the bottleneck​ has always been data. We’re proud to lead this round and back them from a very early stage.”

The round builds on more than €1.18 million (£1 million) from Innovate UK, the Medical Research Council, SBRI, strategic angels and Zinc. It completed a first close of over €2.36 million (£2 million) on 14th October and will close with final investors in the coming weeks.

The round also saw participation from Anamcara Capital, BGV, BY Venture Partners, CentraleSupélec Venture, FJ Labs, Interlace Ventures, True Ventures, and Bpifrance.

“For us, this investment is also a reunion. We backed Nicolas at Scalefast and have seen first-hand how he executes. Backing a founder a second time is one of the clearest signals of conviction an investor can give, and it is not one we give lightly,” said Nico Goulet, Founding Partner, Adara Ventures.

Founded in Strasbourg and incubated at Station F in Paris by Guillaume Nominé and Stehle, Goodweek describes itself as an AI Manager for SMBs. Nominé previously founded Atolia, a collaboration solution he built from his student years through to its sale to JustCall in 2022. Both studied computer science at ENSIIE, and Stehle has mentored Nominé for over a year.

Accenture, whose CEO once argued that promotions will be tied to AI usage/adoption, has now put a hard cap on per-person Claude spending. While it is proving challenging for a firm like Accenture to keep AI spending under control, SMBs find it even harder. The problem Goodweek is solving is that employees have brought AI into SMBs, often without IT approval. This has led to personal accounts, confidential data leaving the company, and duplicate subscriptions adding to costs.

Goodweek solves this problem with a single unified platform bringing together leading AI models, including Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Mistral, while keeping company data isolated and never using it to train third-party models. The company says its platform gives business leaders visibility into who is using which AI tools and at what cost, a metric that has proven difficult to track.

“We want everyone to have a good week at work, powered by AI that’s more accessible, more secure, and genuinely useful day to day. Because AI should be an ally for every employee — not a risk for the company,” said Nominé, CEO and co-founder of Goodweek.

The funding comes just days after the company turned one. In under a year, the company has grown to 50 employees across three countries and counts nearly 150 customers in France, Spain, the United Kingdom, the Benelux, and North America,

Goodweek will use the new capital to scale its sales operations and push into new international markets, including Latin America and Asia.

]]> Munich-based Elevatry, an AI ​​platform for strategic procurement, has closed a €3 million pre-Seed financing round in order to enhance its platform, expand its team, and support market entry in Europe before expanding to North America.

Investors include Bayern Kapital, the management consultancy H&Z, and several business angels, among them Jan Henner-Theißen, Martin Berr-Sorokin, Mike Simon, Markus Ehrle, Andreas Junck, and Alexander Bruehl.

“Strategic purchasing is one of the biggest drivers of results in a company. So far, it’s only being used where there’s sufficient capacity and the necessary expertise,” says Heiko Schwarz, co-founder and CEO of Elevatry. “Our partners handle complex thinking and execute tasks at the highest level. This allows purchasing teams to apply the methodology of their best category managers to every product group. Our investors bring together capital, exclusive purchasing expertise, and market access. From now on, we’ll demonstrate the impact on our customers.”

Elevatry’s financing follows several European funding rounds in AI-powered procurement and related purchasing infrastructure during 2026.

These include Paris-based Pivot’s €34.4 million Series B, Italy’s Soource with €3 million, and German startups Procuros and Finches, which secured €20 million and €2 million, respectively.

Notably, Bayern Kapital also participated in Finches’ pre-Seed round, highlighting an earlier investment in AI-driven procurement technology.

Across eight selected comparable funding announcements covered by EU-Startups this year, approximately €75.5 million has been raised, rising to €78.5 million when Elevatry’s round is included.

“Elevatry combines a highly experienced founding team with a clear vision for the future of strategic procurement. The AI-native platform addresses a significant efficiency and value creation lever within companies, generating immediately tangible customer benefits through the intelligent use of procurement knowledge and data.

“At the same time, the company operates in an attractive, rapidly growing market for AI-powered procurement software. We look forward to supporting the team on its continued growth trajectory together with a strong consortium of business angels,” adds Monika Steger, Managing Director, Bayern Kapital.

Founded in 2026 by Heiko Schwarz, Christian Ruck, and Tizian Ruck and is headquartered near Munich, Elevatry is an AI ​​platform for strategic procurement. Its companions (including Category Strategist, Negotiation Coach, and Risk & Integrity Manager) handle the routine analytical work along the source-to-contract process, providing procurement depth and industry- and commodity-group-specific expertise.

As a system of initiative, the platform plans proactively, prioritises based on impact (€), and prepares proposals – decisions are made collaboratively. Customers configure their own levels of autonomy, approvals, and data sovereignty on an open multi-LLM architecture.

According to the company, strategic procurement significantly influences the costs, quality, resilience, and compliance of the entire purchasing volume.

The potential is substantial: For a company with €1 billion in revenue and €500 million in purchasing volume, a 10 percent improvement can translate into €50 million in additional profit. At a 5 percent margin, this would equate to a doubling of revenue to €2 billion.

In practice, purchasing teams often only have the capacity to actively manage a portion of suppliers and product groups – thus leaving a large part of the potential leverage untapped.

Elevatry sees itself as a system of initiative rather than a system of record. The platform plans proactively, prioritises based on impact in euros, and prepares proposals. Decisions are made collaboratively. Customers configure their own levels of autonomy, approvals, and data sovereignty on an open multi-LLM architecture.

Each result grows into a further optimized knowledge layer that belongs exclusively to the customer.

“We have been supporting Elevatry with great conviction since its founding. Agentic AI will fundamentally change procurement by intelligently automating repetitive knowledge work and effectively supporting decision-making processes,” say Harald Enz and Jonas Harm, Managing Partners of H&Z.

“Elevatry creates a unique combination of leading AI technology and deep procurement domain knowledge. For us, it’s clear: Our clients expect us not only to observe innovation, but to actively shape it and translate it into concrete added value. That’s why we are investing in Elevatry and will closely support the company as a strategic partner on its growth trajectory.”

Elevatry will use today’s funds to further develop its platform and companion portfolio, as well as to implement the accompanying go-to-market activities for market entry. The team will therefore be expanded, particularly in engineering, AI, marketing, and customer support.

The initial focus is on market entry in the DACH region (Germany, Austria, Switzerland) and the EU, with international expansion planned for the medium term, focusing on North America.

 SIE Custom Header — v1.1.2

/* ── Root variables ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
:root {
 --sie-hdr-brand:       #0056b3;        /* SIE brand blue                      */
 --sie-hdr-brand-light: #1a6fc4;
 --sie-hdr-bar-h:       64px;           /* nav bar height — fixed, prevents CLS */

 --sie-hdr-bar-border:  rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.15);
}

.sie-hdr {

 display: block;
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 /* Own stacking context so dropdowns render above Divi page content */
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1000;
}
/* ── Navigation bar ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__bar {
 height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter here — it would trap position:fixed children
 (user-ui mobile bottom bar) inside this element instead of viewport */
 border-bottom: 1px solid var(--sie-hdr-bar-border);
}

 max-width: 1280px;
 height: 100%;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 32px;
}
/* ── Logo ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__logo {
 flex-shrink: 0;
 text-decoration: none;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-img {
 height: 54px;
 width: auto;
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-text {
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 17px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #fff;

}

 padding: 8px 14px;

 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);

 white-space: nowrap;

 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 32px;}
.sie-dest-hero__label{display: block;
 font-size: 13px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.75);
 margin-bottom: 12px;
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-dest-hero__label a{color: inherit;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-dest-hero__label a:hover{color: #fff;
 text-decoration: underline;}
.sie-dest-hero__title{font-size: clamp(32px, 5vw, 56px);
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #ffffff;
 margin: 0 0 14px;
 line-height: 1.1;
 letter-spacing: -0.02em;
 max-width: 800px;}
.sie-dest-hero__tagline{font-size: clamp(15px, 2vw, 19px);
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 margin: 0 0 28px;
 max-width: 1100px;
 line-height: 1.5;
 font-weight: 400;}
.sie-dest-hero__cta{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 8px;
 padding: 12px 24px;
 background: #1E56B0;
 color: #fff;
 font-size: 15px;
 font-weight: 600;
 border-radius: 6px;
 text-decoration: none;
 transition: background 0.2s;}
.sie-dest-hero__cta:hover{background: #163e82;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-dest-hero__actions{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 12px;
 margin-top: 4px;}
.sie-dest-hero__cta--secondary{background: transparent;
 border: 2px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6);
 color: #fff;}
.sie-dest-hero__cta--secondary:hover{background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 border-color: #fff;
 color: #fff;}
.sie-country-heart--hero{position: static !important;
 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 padding: 10px 20px;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 600;
 gap: 8px;
 border-radius: 6px;
 min-width: unset;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.92);
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 border: 2px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.6);
 box-shadow: none;
 backdrop-filter: none;
 white-space: nowrap;
 cursor: pointer;
 font-family: inherit;
 line-height: 1;
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;}
.sie-country-heart--hero:hover{background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.22) !important;
 border-color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.9) !important;
 color: #fff !important;
 transform: none;}
.sie-country-heart--hero.voted{background: rgba(239, 68, 68, 0.28) !important;
 border-color: #f87171 !important;
 color: #fff !important;}
.sie-country-heart--hero.voted i{color: #fca5a5;}
.sie-country-heart--hero .sie-country-heart__count{display: none;
 font-size: 12px;
 opacity: 0.85;}
.sie-country-heart--hero.has-votes .sie-country-heart__count{display: inline;}
.sie-dest-body{max-width: 1100px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px 80px;}
.sie-dest-stats{display: flex;
 flex-wrap: wrap;
 gap: 0;
 background: #f0f4fb;
 border: 1px solid #d4e0f5;
 border-radius: 10px;
 margin: 32px 0;
 overflow: hidden;}
.sie-dest-stat{flex: 1;
 min-width: 150px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 18px 20px;
 border-right: 1px solid #d4e0f5;}
.sie-dest-stat:last-child{border-right: none;}
.sie-dest-stat__label{font-size: 11px;
 font-weight: 600;
 color: #505a6b; 
 text-transform: uppercase;
 letter-spacing: 0.06em;}
.sie-dest-stat__value{font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #003B73;
 line-height: 1.3;}
.sie-admreq-cta-strip .sie-dest-hero__cta{display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 0.5rem;
 padding: 0.75rem 1.5rem;
 background: #fff;
 color: #1d4ed8;
 border-radius: 6px;
 font-weight: 700;
 text-decoration: none;
 font-size: 0.97rem;
 transition: opacity 0.2s;}
.sie-admreq-cta-strip .sie-dest-hero__cta:hover{opacity: 0.9;}

 DESTINATIONS PANEL  — overlay + grid
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
 /* Outer layer: covers full viewport */
 .sie-dest-panel {
 position: fixed;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 2147483000;
 display: flex;
 align-items: stretch;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 opacity: 0;
 visibility: hidden;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .25s ease, visibility .25s;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open {
 opacity: 1;
 visibility: visible;
 pointer-events: auto;
 }
 /* Backdrop */
 .sie-dest-panel__backdrop {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 background: rgba(11, 55, 112, .52);
 backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(3px);
 cursor: pointer;
 }
 /* Sheet — right-panel on desktop */
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1;
 width: min(800px, 100%);
 height: 100%;
 background: #fff;
 overflow-y: auto;
 -webkit-overflow-scrolling: touch;
 padding: 26px 26px 40px;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 gap: 0;
 transform: translateX(28px);
 opacity: 0;
 transition: transform .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1), opacity .38s cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1);
 box-shadow: -20px 0 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateX(0);
 opacity: 1;
 }
 /* Mobile: bottom-sheet */
 @media (max-width: 767px) {
 .sie-dest-panel {
 align-items: flex-end;
 justify-content: stretch;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 width: 100%;
 height: 92vh;
 border-top-left-radius: 22px;
 border-top-right-radius: 22px;
 padding: 20px 16px 40px;
 transform: translateY(28px);
 box-shadow: 0 -16px 48px rgba(0,0,0,.18);
 }
 .sie-dest-panel.open .sie-dest-panel__sheet {
 transform: translateY(0);
 }
 }
 /* ── Header ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__header {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 justify-content: space-between;
 margin-bottom: 6px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__titlewrap {
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 10px;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__globe {
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #1e66f5;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__title {
 font-size: 1.5rem;
 font-weight: 800;
 color: #0b3770;
 margin: 0;
 line-height: 1.2;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close {
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 font-size: 22px;
 color: #0b3770;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 6px 8px;
 border-radius: 8px;
 line-height: 1;
 opacity: .75;
 transition: opacity .15s, background .15s;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__close:hover {
 opacity: 1;
 background: #f0f4ff;
 }
 /* Subheading */
 .sie-dest-panel__sub {
 color: #466087;
 font-size: .94rem;
 margin: 0 0 20px;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 }
 /* ── Country grid ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 display: grid;
 grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);
 gap: 14px;
 /* allow this to grow and scroll */
 flex: 1;
 align-content: start;
 }
 @media (max-width: 620px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr);
 gap: 10px;
 }
 }
 @media (min-width: 621px) and (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-dest-panel__grid {
 grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
 }
 }
 /* ── Country card ── */
 .sie-dest-panel__card {
 position: relative;
 display: block;
 aspect-ratio: 3 / 2;
 border-radius: 12px;
 overflow: hidden;
 text-decoration: none;
 background: #1d3557;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card--no-img .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1d3557 0%, #1e66f5 100%);
 }
 /* Hero image layer — scales on hover */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 transition: transform .4s ease;
 will-change: transform;
 }
 /* <img> fills the card exactly like background-size:cover did.
 loading="lazy" means the browser only fetches each image when the
 panel opens and the card enters the viewport — saving ~30 MB of
 upfront image requests on every page that includes this panel. */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-img {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center;
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-bg,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-bg {
 transform: scale(1.07);
 }
 /* Gradient overlay + text */
 .sie-dest-panel__card-body {
 position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 display: flex;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: flex-end;
 padding: 10px 12px 10px;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .72) 0%,
 rgba(0, 0, 0, .30) 55%,
 transparent 100%
 );
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-name {
 color: #fff;
 font-weight: 700;
 font-size: .92rem;
 line-height: 1.2;
 text-shadow: 0 1px 5px rgba(0,0,0,.55);
 display: block;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 display: block;
 color: rgba(255,255,255,0);
 font-size: .75rem;
 margin-top: 2px;
 transition: color .2s ease, transform .2s ease;
 line-height: 1;
 }
 .sie-dest-panel__card:hover .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow,
 .sie-dest-panel__card:focus-visible .sie-dest-panel__card-arrow {
 color: rgba(255,255,255,.9);
 transform: translateX(4px);
 }
 /* ── Body-scroll lock ── */
 body.sie-dest-panel-open {
 overflow: hidden;
 }
 /* ── Country interest heart ── */
 .sie-country-heart {
 position: absolute;
 top: 8px;
 right: 8px;
 z-index: 10;
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 border: none;
 border-radius: 20px;
 padding: 4px 8px 4px 7px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 cursor: pointer;
 font-size: 13px;
 color: #94a3b8;
 box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.22);
 backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(6px);
 transition: color .18s, transform .18s, background .18s;
 line-height: 1;
 min-width: 28px;
 justify-content: center;
 }
 .sie-country-heart:hover {
 transform: scale(1.12);
 background: #fff;
 color: #ef4444;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted {
 color: #ef4444;
 background: #fff;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.voted i {
 animation: sie-heart-pop .35s cubic-bezier(.36,.07,.19,.97);
 }
 @keyframes sie-heart-pop {
 0%   { transform: scale(1); }
 40%  { transform: scale(1.45); }
 70%  { transform: scale(.88); }
 100% { transform: scale(1); }
 }
 .sie-country-heart__count {
 font-size: 11px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: inherit;
 display: none;
 }
 .sie-country-heart.has-votes .sie-country-heart__count {
 display: inline;
 }
 /* ── Trigger button styles (for use in any menu) ── */
 /* Desktop globe icon */
 .se-dest-desktop-btn {
 font-size: 24px;
 color: #fff;
 text-decoration: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 transition: transform .2s, color .2s;
 position: relative;
 line-height: 1;
 background: transparent;
 border: 0;
 padding: 0;
 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover {
 transform: scale(1.15);
 color: #FFCC00;
 }
 /* Tooltip on desktop */
 @media (min-width: 1024px) {
 .se-dest-desktop-btn::after {
 content: "Study Destinations";
 position: absolute;
 bottom: -30px;
 left: 50%;
 transform: translateX(-50%);
 background: #007BFF;
 color: #fff;
 padding: 4px 8px;
 font-size: 12px;
 border-radius: 5px;
 opacity: 0;
 pointer-events: none;
 transition: opacity .2s;
 white-space: nowrap;
 }
 .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover::after {
 opacity: 1;
 }
 }
 /* Mobile pill button */
 .se-dest-btn {
 background: #0b3770 !important;
 color: #fff !important;
 }
 .se-dest-btn:hover {
 background: #1e66f5 !important;

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

                        </div>
                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__RECTORS_Q1.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has a strategy and an overarching structure supporting internationalisation</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The internationalisation strategy is available and prominently displayed on your website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Internationalisation is an important driver for institutional change, and has a great influence on the major activities of a higher education institution (HEI) i.e. education and research. The importance of internationalisation is recognised, and most institutions have a strategy for internationalisation. However, for a strategy to be efficient, and for it to drive the HEI's activities regarding internationalisation, there is a need for its acceptance from across the whole institution. In addition the strategy could also be accessible to external collaborative partners. It is highly important to have the institution's internationalisation and modernisation strategy published and easily accessible to all.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries. The activities and co-operation projects agreed by the HEI should be based on identified needs. In addition they should identify geographical and subject priorities of the internationalisation strategy.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Specific support measures are provided to staff working at all levels of the institution with outgoing and incoming participants. For example:  allocation of additional resources, training on intercultural competences and other relevant aspects of the mob</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution should allocate additional resources to support staff working at all levels of the institution with outgoing and incoming participants, such as allowing staff adequate time to carry out work with outgoing and incoming participants and providing administrative back-up (e.g. with financial management). Trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, management of mobility projects’, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Incentives are provided to staff involved in international activities</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Participation in such international projects should be seen as an important aspect of the professional development of the staff and of the modernisation of the HEI. It should, therefore, be considered a key component in staff evaluation. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels to encourage and recognise staff participating in such projects, as well as allow adequate time to carry out this work.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-case">
                                                <h3>Case studies</h3>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/the-effective-management-and-ownership-of-erasmus-for-internationalisation" target="_blank">The effective management and ownership of Erasmus +’ for ‘internationalisation’</a></div>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/internationalisation-at-the-university-of-helsinki" target="_blank">Internationalisation at the University of Helsinki </a></div>
                                             </div>
                    <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close-text"><i class="fa fa-times fa-2x"></i><span>Close</span></div>
                </div>
            </div>
                         <div class="eche-report-full-question-wrapper">
                <div class="eche-officer-question-title-wrapper">
                    <div class="eche-report-title-icons-wrapper">
                                                 <div class="eche-report-officer-number">
                            <img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/eche-pdf/number-corner-orange-2.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">

                            <div class="eche-report-officer-number-text">2</div>
                        </div>
                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__OFFICERS_Q2.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>
                    </div>
                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has established a framework of Inter-Institutional Agreements for Erasmus+ mobility</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on areas of mutual interest</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is vital that Inter-Institutional Agreements are based on areas of mutual interest. These agreements should identify shared quality requirements specific to the planned exchanges, including concrete proposals as to how these activities will contribute to the development of learning and teaching in participating institutions. The involvement of academic staff is key to ensuring that the selection of partners is based on sufficient knowledge of the area. Each HEI should decide who is responsible for initiating, signing and implementing these agreements and the list of responsible persons should be available on the website for contact and consultation purposes.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on the compatibility of study programmes</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Inter-Institutional Agreements should be based on a comprehensive understanding of the partner HEIs, the compatibility of study programmes, quality levels and standards considered adequate for student and staff mobility activities. For example, selected partners should have learning, teaching and assessment procedures that can be accepted by the sending institution without requiring mobile students to do any additional work or take examinations upon returning from the receiving institution. The compatibility of the programmes should be reflected in the learning outcomes to be achieved.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on shared quality requirements, student and staff selection for mobility and clear timelines at all stages of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>A key role of Inter-Institutional Agreements is to set out agreed, shared quality criteria and clear timelines for all stages of the mobility.<br>Shared quality criteria may include, but are not limited to: selection criteria for the nomination of students and staff, recommended language skills, grading systems, measures for preparing, receiving and integrating Erasmus+ participants. These might be expanded with geographic and subject-specific criteria.<br>In terms of the timelines set out for the mobility activities, particular attention should be paid to:</p><ul><li>The nomination of mobile students by the sending HEI,</li><li>The acceptance of nominees, and</li><li>The issuing of the Transcript of Records after the study period abroad by the receiving HEI. This is normally issued within five weeks after the end date of the mobility period.</li></ul>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-case">
                                                <h3>Case studies</h3>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/establishing-a-framework-of-inter-institutional-agreements-for-international-erasmus-mobility" target="_blank">Establishing a framework of Inter-Institutional Agreements for international Erasmus+ mobility</a></div>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/inter-institutional-agreements" target="_blank">Inter-Institutional Agreements</a></div>
                                             </div>
                    <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close-text"><i class="fa fa-times fa-2x"></i><span>Close</span></div>
                </div>
            </div>
                         <div class="eche-report-full-question-wrapper">
                <div class="eche-officer-question-title-wrapper">
                    <div class="eche-report-title-icons-wrapper">
                                                 <div class="eche-report-officer-number">
                            <img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/eche-pdf/number-corner-orange-3.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">

                            <div class="eche-report-officer-number-text">3</div>
                        </div>
                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__OFFICERS_Q3.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>
                    </div>
                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution expresses its commitment to equal access and opportunities to mobile participants</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">There are specific provisions e.g. in the general policies, rules and regulations of the institution</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In signing the Erasmus Charter for Higher Education, the institution agrees to respect <strong>in full</strong> the principles of non-discrimination as set out in the Programme. The institution must clearly demonstrate through its policies, rules and regulations that equal access and opportunities to mobile participants from all backgrounds. Which means that all individuals or groups will be treated equally, irrespective of their characteristics. In accordance with Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, there should be no discrimination "based on sex, race, colour, ethnic or social origin, genetic features, language, religion or belief, political or any other opinion, membership of a national minority, property, birth, disability, age or sexual orientation". For more information, see: <a href="http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf">http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf</a></p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The principle - that extra fees are not being charged to incoming mobile students - is implemented</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The receiving institution must <strong>not </strong>charge any type of fees to incoming mobility students for the tuition, registration or examination of these students or for their access to laboratory, library and other facilities offered to local students.<br>In certain cases, however, mobile students may be required to pay small fees for insurance, student unions, use of miscellaneous materials (e.g. photocopies, laboratory products) on the same basis as these are charged to local students. Students should be made aware of these extra costs before the start of mobility. Fees may only be charged in the case of full degree mobility or for students registered in joint degree programmes.&nbsp;</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">All students and staff (incoming and outgoing) are treated equally in all academic and service matters</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In accordance with equal access and opportunities, all students and staff should be treated equally in all academic and service matters. Clear appeal procedures should be in place to ensure equal treatment. There should be individuals - such as mentors and counsellors - available to offer support.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It provides incoming mobile participants with access to the same services and facilities available to local students and staff</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is vital to ensure that incoming mobility participants have full access to the same services and facilities as local students and staff. For example, mobility participants with special needs can benefit from the support services that the receiving institution offers to its local students and staff.</p>                      </div>

                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Ensuring that the mobile participant, sending and receiving HEI/organisation/enterprise (i.e. all three parties) sign the Learning Agreement before the start of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The purpose of the Learning Agreement is to provide a transparent and efficient preparation of the study period abroad and to ensure that the student will receive recognition in his/her degree for the educational components or traineeship successfully completed abroad. The Learning Agreement:</p><ul><li>Sets out the learning outcomes for the mobility, including both the educational components or traineeship activities to be carried out by the student at the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise, which will be recognised by the sending institution upon successful completion of the study programme abroad and counted towards his/her degree.</li><li>Ensures full recognition for satisfactorily completed activities of study mobility and traineeships in terms of credits awarded, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams, and documents these credits in the student records, so that they can be identified in a transparent way.</li></ul><p>The Learning Agreement is binding for all parties and constitutes the cornerstone of successful student mobility (for studies, traineeships, and combinations thereof), including quality assurances and the process for transparent transfer of credits.         <h2 class="eche-report-section-title eche-pdf-page-break">During the mobility</h2>
        <div class="eche-report-section-wrapper">

                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">

                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It provides opportunities for incoming mobile participants to share their culture and experiences with their peers inside and with the local community</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Incoming mobile students also bring new perspectives to the institution, the local students and the culture which is part of the internationalisation of the receiving institution. This is a significant opportunity to benefit from the experiences that international students bring. To capitalise on these experiences, the institution and its student organisations should put in place opportunities for incoming students to showcase their talent and perspectives through access to existing local initiatives (e.g. school teaching programmes, community projects) and setting up new initiatives to celebrate the different cultures (e.g. theatre performances, food and cultural weeks etc.). Local associations can support the integration of incoming students with the local community, through existing initiatives such as the Social Erasmus and Erasmus in School projects (<a href="http://socialerasmus.esn.org">http://socialerasmus.esn.org</a>).&nbsp;</p><p>Some incoming students may even have been involved in the management or governance of their sending institutions and recognising this opportunity and involving incoming students in similar functions in the receiving institution such as in the student union (elected representative) or working groups dedicated to the voice of the international student.&nbsp; &nbsp;</p>                      </div>

        <h2 class="eche-report-section-title eche-pdf-page-break">After the mobility</h2>
        <div class="eche-report-section-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-report-full-question-wrapper">
                <div class="eche-officer-question-title-wrapper">
                    <div class="eche-report-title-icons-wrapper">
                                                 <div class="eche-report-officer-number">
                            <img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/eche-pdf/number-corner-orange-11.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">

                            <div class="eche-report-officer-number-text">11</div>
                        </div>
                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__OFFICERS_Q11.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>
                    </div>
                    <div class="eche-report-title-question-text-wrapper">
                        <div class="eche-officer-question"> At the end of the mobility, your institution has formal procedures for recognising student mobility (good practices linked to recognition at the end of the mobility, e.g. in the use of Transcripts of Records and Grade Distribution Tables)</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Transcripts of Records are issued in a timely manner (normally 5 weeks) to both incoming and outgoing students</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is highly important in the recognition framework to provide Transcripts of Records in a timely manner, immediately following the mobility period. After the mobility, the receiving institution should send a Transcript of Records to the student and to the sending institution within a period stipulated in the Inter-Institutional Agreement (normally within five weeks after publication/proclamation of the student’s results at the receiving institution). It can be provided electronically or through any other means accessible to the student and the sending institution. The Transcript of Records from the receiving institution should refer to the educational components agreed upon in the Learning Agreement. Grade distribution information should be included as well, either as a web link or an annex.</p><p>Following the receipt of the Transcript of Records from the receiving institution, the sending institution should automatically transfer and recognise the student’s academic outcomes successfully completed at the receiving institution, as agreed in the Learning Agreement, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams. The Sending Institution will provide a Transcript of Records to the student or record the results in a database or any other means accessible to the student, normally within five weeks after having received the transcript of the receiving institution. The EU official template for the Learning Agreement for studies (including the Transcript of Records) is available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm</a></p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Transcripts of Records of incoming students include, where applicable, a Grade Distribution Table for the programme of study, according to the ECTS Users’ Guide</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Where applicable, the Sending Institution should translate the grades received by the student abroad. To enable the Sending Institution to do so, it is highly important for the receiving institution to provide a clear explanation of the institutional grading system and grade distribution in the department or study programme together with the Transcript of Records. Such information can be provided either through a web link or as an annex to the Transcripts of Records. Where applicable, use should be made of a Grade Distribution Table for the programme of study, according to the ECTS Users’ Guide (<a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/ects/users-guide/index.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/ects/users-guide/index.htm</a>).</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">All credits gained by students during a period of study abroad that were specified in the final version of the Learning Agreement are automatically transferred by your institution and count towards the students' final degree, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The sending institution should ensure that all the credits earned by the mobile student during the mobility period are recognised and counted towards the final degree, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams. The period of study abroad must be clear in the student's records and documents issued to the student (Diploma Supplement or equivalent). This is a golden rule of recognition of credit mobility within the framework of inter-institutional agreements. All the credits towards the student's degree that are earned during the mobility period and which were originally agreed on in the Learning Agreement (or a revised version to it) should be recognised by the sending HEI without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams. Learning Agreements are binding for all the parties and require that, on successful completion of the mobility period, the sending HEI recognises credits earned by the student and documents these credits in the student records, so they can be identified in a transparent way.</p><p>Upon receipt of the Transcript of Records or Training Certificates, the sending HEI should:<br>a) certify the mobile student has fulfilled all requirements stipulated in the Learning Agreement;<br>b) ensure recognition of the mobility period abroad within the time-scale and according to the conditions stipulated in the institutional recognition framework.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">In addition to recognising formal learning, the institution recognises any non-formal or informal learning acquired during the mobility according to the ECTS Users’ Guide, e.g. by awarding ECTS credits for volunteering</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>During a period of mobility, students often take advantage of other opportunities outside of their required courses. These may include specific activities which can be considered non-formal or informal learning where they have acquired new skills. This could include additional language and cultural courses, extra-curricular activities, setting up a business and volunteer work undertaken by the student in that period or upon return at the receiving institution.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-case">
                                                <h3>Case studies</h3>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/standing-out-from-the-crowd-supporting-students-through-full-recognition-and-documenting-of-mobility-outcomes" target="_blank">"Standing out from the crowd" - supporting students through full recognition and documenting of mobility outcomes</a></div>
                                                <div><a href="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/eche/a-common-approach-to-ects-grade-conversion-ensuring-a-fair-assessment-of-student-performance-after-study-abroad" target="_blank">A common approach to ECTS grade conversion, ensuring a fair assessment of student performance after study abroad</a></div>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question-icon"><img class="eche-report-question-icon" src="https://erasmus-plus.ec.europa.eu/profiles/custom/eac_profile/modules/eac_eche/images/ECHE__OFFICERS_Q12.png" width="100%" height="100%" alt="Question Icon" title="Question Icon" loading="lazy">
</div>
